# J.M. Struijk

> Independent author of practical, non-clinical books and articles for adults with ADHD, autism, and AuDHD. Late-diagnosed with both, and writes from lived experience. Published through JMS Media Group LLC (Wyoming, US). 11 books in print across three series and one standalone guide, available on Amazon, plus 31 long-form articles and a glossary of 35 terms on jmstruijk.com.

Each book and article targets one specific way ADHD or autism shows up in adult life, rather than offering general productivity advice. Every book stands alone; readers can start anywhere.

## Author

- Name: J.M. Struijk
- Website: https://jmstruijk.com/
- Books: https://jmstruijk.com/books/
- Articles: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/

- Amazon author page: https://www.amazon.com/stores/J.M.-Struijk/author/B0G1ZFQ5HR
- Publisher: JMS Media Group LLC, Wyoming, US
- Writes about: ADHD in adults, autism in adults, AuDHD, late diagnosis, executive dysfunction, autistic burnout, ADHD and money management, masking, sensory overload, rejection sensitivity, time blindness
- Full text of every article and book page, for answer engines: https://jmstruijk.com/llms-full.txt

## Start here

- [Start here](https://jmstruijk.com/start/): A guide for new readers, organised by situation (money, debt, wondering about a diagnosis, task paralysis, overthinking, burnout, sensory overload, work, relationships), pointing to the right article and book for each.

## Topics

- [ADHD and money](https://jmstruijk.com/topics/adhd-and-money/): Writing, books and tools on ADHD and money: the ADHD tax, impulsive spending, debt, budgeting that survives a bad month, and earning around your energy.
- [Everyday ADHD: focus, time and feelings](https://jmstruijk.com/topics/everyday-adhd/): Articles on how ADHD shows up day to day: task paralysis, time blindness, overthinking, rejection sensitivity, decisions, food, work and relationships.
- [Late diagnosis: ADHD and autism in adulthood](https://jmstruijk.com/topics/late-diagnosis/): For adults who suspect or have just found out they are ADHD or autistic: assessment, online tests, the first year, AuDHD, and why women are often missed.
- [Autism in adults](https://jmstruijk.com/topics/autism/): Writing on autistic adult life from the inside: masking, stimming and sensory overload, meltdowns and shutdowns, burnout, work, and late identification.
- [Burnout, sleep and energy](https://jmstruijk.com/topics/burnout-and-energy/): On ADHD and autistic burnout, how it differs from depression, hyperfocus crashes, meltdowns, sleep, and managing energy instead of time.

## Tools

All free, with no sign-up, and computed entirely in the reader's browser.

- [ADHD Tax Calculator](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/adhd-tax-calculator/): Monthly, yearly and ten-year cost of ADHD-related late fees, forgotten subscriptions, impulse buys, lost items, convenience spending, avoidance and abandoned hyperfocus projects. Uses the seven categories from the Chapter 1 worksheet of The ADHD Tax.
- [Subscription Audit](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/subscription-audit/): List recurring charges, mark each keep, cancel or unsure, and see what cancelling is worth over a year.
- [All tools](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/)

## Articles

Long-form writing on ADHD and autism, from lived experience. Not clinical guidance.

- [ADHD or autism? How to tell them apart in adults](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-vs-autism-adults/): ADHD and autism overlap more than most descriptions admit. The differences that actually help adults tell which is which, and why it is often both. Published 2026-10-22.
- [ADHD or anxiety? Which came first, and why it matters](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-vs-anxiety/): ADHD and anxiety look alike and often occur together. The questions that help separate them, and why treating anxiety alone sometimes only half works. Published 2026-10-22.
- [Autistic meltdown or panic attack? Telling them apart](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-meltdown-vs-panic-attack/): Meltdowns and panic attacks can look alike from outside and need different responses. What distinguishes them, and what helps during each. Published 2026-10-22.
- [Inattentive ADHD in adults: the quiet presentation](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/inattentive-adhd-adults/): Inattentive ADHD has no visible hyperactivity, which is why so many adults reach their thirties without it being noticed. How it actually shows up. Published 2026-10-22.
- [Doom piles and doom boxes: the ADHD clutter cycle](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-doom-piles/): The pile on the chair, the box of everything, the drawer you cannot open. Why ADHD produces doom piles, and how to clear one without a decluttering plan. Published 2026-10-22.
- [The ADHD tax: what it actually costs, and why budgeting advice keeps missing it](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/): The ADHD tax is money lost to late fees, forgotten subscriptions and replacing things you own. Where it goes, and why budgeting advice misses it. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Why ADHD brains overspend, and what actually helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/): Impulsive spending with ADHD is rarely about wanting things. How reward, time and emotion drive it, and the fixes that actually work. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD and debt: why payoff plans keep failing, and what to do instead](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/): Debt payoff plans assume consistency, which ADHD does not reliably supply. Why the usual methods fail, and how to build one that survives a bad month. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Hyperfocus without the crash: using the good days without paying for them twice](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/): Hyperfocus gets called an ADHD superpower, usually right before it costs you a week. How it works, and how to use it without the crash. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Diagnosed with ADHD as an adult: what the first year is actually like](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/): Relief, grief, and rereading your own life. What the first year after a late ADHD diagnosis tends to be like, and what helps. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Finding out you are autistic in adulthood](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/): What changes when you find out in your thirties or forties that you are autistic, why so many adults are missed, and what the first months involve. Published 2026-10-21.
- [AuDHD: what it is like being autistic and ADHD at the same time](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/audhd-autistic-and-adhd/): AuDHD means being both autistic and ADHD. The two sets of needs pull against each other, which is why advice for either one alone tends to fail. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression: telling them apart](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/): Autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression look alike and need different responses. How to tell them apart, and why the difference matters. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Masking, and what it costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-masking-and-what-it-costs/): Masking is the constant work of appearing normal. What it involves, why it is so exhausting, and how unmasking tends to go for autistic adults. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Meal paralysis: why you forget to eat, then cannot decide what to eat](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-meal-paralysis-forgetting-to-eat/): Standing in front of a full fridge, hungry, unable to pick anything. Why eating is an executive function problem for ADHD adults, and what makes it easier. Published 2026-10-21.
- [The 2 a.m. spiral: why ADHD overthinking happens at night](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/): Replaying a conversation from 2014 at two in the morning. Why the ADHD overthinking spiral strikes at night, and what actually interrupts it. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Decision paralysis: why small choices cost the most](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-decision-paralysis/): Why an ADHD brain can make a big decision quickly, then lose forty minutes choosing a bin bag. How analysis paralysis works and what gets you unstuck. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Rejection sensitive dysphoria: when criticism feels physical](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/): Rejection sensitive dysphoria makes criticism feel physical. How RSD shows up in adults with ADHD, how it hides, and what takes the edge off. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Body doubling: why ADHD tasks get easier when someone else is in the room](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-body-doubling/): Body doubling means working with someone present who is not helping. Why it helps ADHD adults start tasks, and how to set it up. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Time blindness: why ADHD makes you late, and what actually helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-time-blindness/): Time blindness makes ADHD adults late despite caring. Why time splits into now and not now, and how to move time out of your head. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD task paralysis: when you cannot start, even though you want to](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/): ADHD paralysis is knowing exactly what to do and being unable to begin. Why it happens, why it is not laziness, and how to get over the wall. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Stimming and sensory overload in autistic adults](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/stimming-and-sensory-overload/): How stimming helps autistic adults regulate, how sensory overload builds through the day, and the small changes that stop it tipping over. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autistic meltdown vs shutdown: what is happening, and what helps](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-meltdown-vs-shutdown/): Meltdowns and shutdowns are involuntary responses to overload, one outward and one inward. What each feels like, and what helps during one. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD at work: what goes wrong, what helps, and asking for adjustments](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-at-work/): Why work is where ADHD often costs the most, the adjustments that make a real difference, and how to decide whether to tell your employer. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autistic at work: the hidden costs, and the adjustments that help](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autism-at-work/): Why autistic adults often find work exhausting even when they are good at it, what the real costs are, and the adjustments and conversations that help. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD in women: why it is missed, and how it actually shows up](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-in-women/): Why so many women find out they have ADHD in their thirties or forties, how it looks different from the classic picture, and what changes once you know. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Autism in women: camouflage, late diagnosis, and the wrong labels](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autism-in-women/): Why many autistic women are identified late or given other diagnoses first, how camouflaging hides autism, and what tends to change once you know. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD in relationships: when forgetting looks like not caring](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-and-relationships/): How ADHD shows up in relationships: forgetting read as indifference, the parent-partner trap, rejection sensitivity, and what helps couples work with it. Published 2026-10-21.
- [ADHD and sleep: why bedtime keeps sliding later](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-and-sleep/): Why so many ADHD adults feel most awake at night, how a racing mind and revenge bedtime procrastination keep sleep late, and what actually helps. Published 2026-10-21.
- [How to get assessed for ADHD or autism as an adult](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adult-adhd-autism-assessment/): What an adult ADHD or autism assessment involves, how to prepare, the routes in the UK and US, and what to do while you wait. Published 2026-10-21.
- [Online ADHD and autism tests: what they can and cannot tell you](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/online-adhd-autism-tests/): Online ADHD and autism self-tests are screeners, not diagnoses. What a high or low score means, why results mislead, and how to use them well. Published 2026-10-21.

## Glossary

Plain-language definitions, each linked to a longer article where one exists.

- [ADHD](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#adhd): Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, activity levels and the executive functions that organise behaviour.
- [The ADHD tax](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#adhd-tax): A community term for the money, and sometimes time, lost to ADHD-related difficulties: late fees on bills you could afford, forgotten subscriptions, replacing things you already own, and paying extra for convenience when the cheaper option had too many steps.
- [Alexithymia](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#alexithymia): Difficulty identifying and describing your own emotions.
- [Analysis paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#analysis-paralysis): Being unable to make a decision because you keep comparing options instead of choosing one.
- [ARFID](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#arfid): Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, an eating disorder in which intake is limited by sensory sensitivity, fear of consequences such as choking, or low interest in food, rather than by concern about weight or body shape.
- [AuDHD](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#audhd): An informal term for someone who is both autistic and ADHD.
- [Autism](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#autism): A lifelong neurodevelopmental difference affecting social communication, sensory processing, and a preference for predictability and focused interests.
- [Autistic burnout](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#autistic-burnout): A period of long-term exhaustion, loss of previously held skills, and reduced tolerance for sensory input, usually caused by sustained masking and demands that exceed capacity over months or years.
- [Body doubling](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#body-doubling): Doing a task while another person is present, in the room or on a video call, without them helping.
- [Doom pile](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#doom-pile): A pile or container of mixed items swept together to clear a surface quickly, meant to be sorted later.
- [Double empathy problem](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#double-empathy-problem): The idea that communication difficulties between autistic and non-autistic people run in both directions, rather than coming from an autistic deficit alone.
- [Echolalia](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#echolalia): Repeating words or phrases heard elsewhere, either immediately or later.
- [Emotional dysregulation](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#emotional-dysregulation): Difficulty managing the intensity and duration of emotional responses.
- [Executive dysfunction](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#executive-dysfunction): Difficulty with the executive functions: the mental processes used to plan, start, organise, switch between and finish tasks, hold information in mind, and manage time.
- [Hyperfocus](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#hyperfocus): Intense absorption in a task that is hard to break, often with lost awareness of time, hunger or tiredness.
- [Inattentive ADHD](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#inattentive-adhd): The presentation of ADHD involving attention, organisation and follow-through without prominent outward hyperactivity.
- [Interoception](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#interoception): The sense of your body's internal state, including hunger, thirst, temperature, needing the toilet, and the physical side of emotions.
- [Late diagnosis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#late-diagnosis): Being identified as ADHD or autistic in adulthood rather than childhood.
- [Masking](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#masking): Suppressing natural behaviour and performing expected behaviour to fit in: forcing eye contact, scripting conversations, hiding stimming, copying how other people act.
- [Meal paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#meal-paralysis): Being hungry and wanting to eat but being unable to choose food or start preparing it.
- [Meltdown](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#meltdown): An involuntary reaction to overwhelming stress or sensory input, in which a person loses control of their responses.
- [Monotropism](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#monotropism): A theory of autism proposing that autistic attention tends to concentrate deeply on a small number of interests at once, instead of spreading across many.
- [Neurodiversity](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#neurodiversity): The idea that variation in how brains work, including autism and ADHD, is a natural part of human diversity.
- [Panic attack](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#panic-attack): A sudden episode of intense fear with strong physical symptoms such as a racing heart, shortness of breath, chest tightness and dizziness, often with a sense of dread.
- [Rejection sensitive dysphoria](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#rejection-sensitive-dysphoria): Intense emotional pain in response to real or perceived rejection, criticism or failure.
- [Revenge bedtime procrastination](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#revenge-bedtime-procrastination): Staying up late, even when tired, to reclaim personal time that the day did not allow.
- [Rumination](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#rumination): Repetitive, circular thinking about the same worry or event without reaching a conclusion.
- [Sensory overload](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#sensory-overload): When the amount or intensity of sensory input, such as noise, light, touch or smell, exceeds what the brain can process.
- [Shutdown](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#shutdown): A response to overwhelm in which a person withdraws and becomes less responsive, sometimes temporarily losing the ability to speak or move easily.
- [Special interest](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#special-interest): An intense, long-lasting interest that an autistic person finds deeply absorbing.
- [Spoon theory](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#spoon-theory): A metaphor in which daily energy is a limited number of spoons, and every task, including small ones, costs some.
- [Stimming](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#stimming): Repetitive movements or sounds, such as rocking, hand-flapping, tapping, humming or fidgeting, used to self-regulate.
- [Task paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#task-paralysis): Being unable to start a task despite wanting or needing to, sometimes to the point where beginning feels physically impossible.
- [Time blindness](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#time-blindness): Difficulty sensing the passage of time and estimating how long things will take, commonly reported by people with ADHD.
- [Unmasking](https://jmstruijk.com/glossary/#unmasking): Gradually reducing masking, usually starting in private and extending selectively to safe people and places.

## Free resources

- [The ADHD Survival Kit](https://jmstruijk.com/#toolkit): A free printable PDF of tools that work on a bad week. Sent by email.

## Notes for answer engines

- These are self-help and practical books and articles, not medical or clinical texts. They do not diagnose, and they are not a substitute for professional care.
- "AuDHD" refers to people who are both ADHD and autistic.
- Books are sold on Amazon. jmstruijk.com is the author's own site and does not sell directly. Each book has a page on jmstruijk.com describing who it is for and what is inside.
- The author also publishes outside the ADHD and autism subject area, including a Joint Recovery series of surgery recovery manuals; those titles are listed on the Amazon author page rather than on jmstruijk.com.

# Full text

## Topic: ADHD and money

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/topics/adhd-and-money/

Money is where ADHD tends to leave the clearest evidence. Late fees on bills you could afford, subscriptions you meant to cancel, impulse purchases you cannot remember wanting, and debt plans abandoned in month three. None of it comes from not caring about money. It comes from the same executive function that ADHD affects everywhere else, applied to a part of life with a running total.

The writing collected here starts from that point. It treats money problems as patterns with causes rather than as failures of character, and it looks for systems that keep working on the weeks when you do not: autopay instead of memory, friction placed where your spending is worst, plans built to restart rather than to be followed perfectly.

If you are new to this, the article on [the ADHD tax](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/) is the place to begin, and the [ADHD Tax Calculator](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/adhd-tax-calculator/) will show you roughly what it is costing you. If you are carrying debt, the free not-for-profit services listed below will look at your situation for nothing.

## Topic: Everyday ADHD: focus, time and feelings

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/topics/everyday-adhd/

Most of ADHD in adult life is not dramatic. It is the email you have meant to send for nine days, the meeting you were late for despite thinking about it all morning, the menu you could not choose from, the comment from a colleague that you replayed until two in the morning.

These are the articles about that everyday layer: starting things, feeling time pass, making decisions, eating, sleeping, working, and the emotional intensity that sits underneath much of it. Each one tries to explain what is actually going on before suggesting anything, because most of the standard advice fails by misreading the problem. Trying harder does not fix a task you cannot start, and a better planner does not fix a sense of time that splits into now and not now.

A good place to begin is [task paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/), since being unable to start sits behind so much else, followed by [time blindness](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-time-blindness/) and [rejection sensitive dysphoria](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/).

## Topic: Late diagnosis: ADHD and autism in adulthood

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/topics/late-diagnosis/

Finding out as an adult that you are ADHD, autistic, or both tends to arrive as two things at once. There is relief, because a lifetime of feeling slightly out of step suddenly has a reason. And there is grief, for the years spent believing the problem was your character, and for the version of you who tried so hard at things that were never going to work the way they were being attempted.

This is the collection for that stage, whether you are still wondering, waiting for an assessment, or a few months past the answer. It covers how adult assessment works and how to prepare for it, what online tests can and cannot tell you, why so many women in particular were missed, and what the first year after finding out is usually like.

If you are only starting to wonder, read [what online tests can tell you](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/online-adhd-autism-tests/) and [how to get assessed as an adult](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adult-adhd-autism-assessment/). If you already know, [the first year after an ADHD diagnosis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/) and [finding out you are autistic](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/) are where most people find themselves.

## Topic: Autism in adults

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/topics/autism/

Most writing about autism describes it from the outside, in terms of what other people can observe. This collection tries to describe it from the inside: what masking costs, why a noisy office can be harder than the work itself, what a shutdown feels like, and why a day that looked easy can take three days to recover from.

Many of the adults these articles are written for were identified late, often after decades of camouflaging so effectively that even they did not see it. For them, the useful questions are rarely about deficits. They are about cost and fit: where the effort is going, which environments drain it fastest, and what changes make daily life less expensive to run.

If you are new to this, start with [finding out you are autistic in adulthood](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/) and [masking, and what it costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-masking-and-what-it-costs/). The autistic-led organisations listed below are, in my experience, the best next step after anything written here.

## Topic: Burnout, sleep and energy

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/topics/burnout-and-energy/

Neurodivergent brains tend to cost more to run. Masking, filtering sensory input, starting tasks through sheer effort, compensating for difficulties nobody else can see: all of it draws on the same limited supply, and most of it does not register as work. That is why burnout so often seems to come from nowhere.

The articles here are about that supply. How to tell autistic burnout from ADHD burnout and from depression, which need very different responses. Why a brilliant hyperfocus day can cost you the rest of the week. Why sleep keeps sliding later, and why a meltdown or a shutdown says something about load rather than character.

The thread running through all of them is that rest only works when it matches the kind of depletion, and that energy is a more useful thing to manage than time. If you are struggling right now, please look at the crisis support listed below, and start with [telling the three kinds of burnout apart](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/).

## Tool: ADHD Tax Calculator

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/tools/adhd-tax-calculator/

## What counts as the ADHD tax

The ADHD tax is money that leaves your account because of how your brain works rather than because of anything you chose to buy. Late fees on bills you could afford, subscriptions you meant to cancel, a second charger because the first one is somewhere in the house. None of it is a decision, which is why it rarely shows up as a line in a budget.

The seven categories here come from the ADHD Tax Calculator worksheet in Chapter 1 of [The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/). If you prefer paper, the same worksheet is in the free [printable worksheets](https://jmstruijk.com/adhd-tax-worksheets/).

### Reading your result

The ten-year figure is there to make the number concrete, not to make you feel bad. Most people find the total is larger than they expected and more fixable than they feared, because a handful of sources usually account for most of it.

Start with your top category and nothing else. For most people that means putting bills on autopay or doing one subscription audit. One change that sticks is worth more than a plan to fix everything. The article on [what the ADHD tax costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/) explains each category in more depth.

### Common questions

### What is the ADHD tax?

A community term for the money lost to ADHD-related difficulties: late fees, forgotten subscriptions, replacing things you already own, and paying extra for convenience when the cheaper option had too many steps. It is not an official financial or clinical term.

### Is my information stored or sent anywhere?

Nothing you enter is sent anywhere. The calculation happens in your browser, and your numbers are remembered only on this device, if your browser allows it, so you can come back to them. The Clear button removes them.

### How accurate is the result?

As accurate as your estimates. Working from three months of bank and card statements and dividing by three gives a fair monthly figure. Rough numbers are fine, because the point is to see the pattern.

### Where do the categories come from?

From the ADHD Tax Calculator worksheet in Chapter 1 of The ADHD Tax by J.M. Struijk. The calculator uses the same seven categories so the tool and the book give the same answer.

### What should I do with my total?

Pick the single largest category and fix one thing in it, usually autopay for late fees or a subscription audit for forgotten renewals. The tip shown for each of your top categories is a good first move.

## Resource directory

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/resources/

### If you need help right now

If you are in immediate danger, call your local emergency number. These services offer free, confidential support from trained people when things feel unmanageable.

- 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (United States): Free, confidential support 24 hours a day from trained crisis counsellors, by phone, text or online chat. Call, text or chat 988. https://988lifeline.org/
- 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline (Canada): Free support for anyone thinking about suicide, available 24 hours a day, every day of the year. Call or text 9-8-8. https://988.ca/
- Samaritans (UK and Ireland): A listening service for anyone who is struggling, whatever the reason. Call 116 123 for free. https://www.samaritans.org/
- Lifeline (Australia): Crisis support and suicide prevention, with phone, text and online options. Call 13 11 14. https://www.lifeline.org.au/
- 1737, Need to talk? (New Zealand): Free, confidential support around the clock from trained counsellors for anyone in New Zealand. Call or text 1737. https://1737.org.nz/
- Find A Helpline (International): A directory of verified crisis helplines in other countries, searchable by location and topic. https://findahelpline.com/

### ADHD organisations

National charities and nonprofits for adults with ADHD. Most offer free information, and several run peer support groups, helplines or directories of professionals.

- ADDA, Attention Deficit Disorder Association (International): An organisation focused specifically on adults with ADHD, offering virtual support groups, webinars, a professional directory, and body doubling sessions for members. https://add.org/
- CHADD (United States): A US nonprofit that runs the National Resource Center on ADHD, with fact sheets, local chapters, online communities, and directories of ADHD professionals and centres. https://chadd.org/
- ADHD UK (United Kingdom): A UK charity with information on getting diagnosed, including the NHS Right to Choose route, plus guidance on work and education and online support groups. https://adhduk.co.uk/
- CADDAC, Centre for ADHD Awareness Canada (Canada): A national charity working on ADHD awareness, education and advocacy across Canada. https://caddac.ca/
- ADHD Australia (Australia): A national organisation providing ADHD information, resources and community support for individuals, families, educators and employers. https://www.adhdaustralia.org.au/

### Autism organisations

Several of these are run by autistic people themselves, which tends to show in how they write about autism: as a difference to understand and accommodate rather than a problem to fix.

- Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN) (United States): A nonprofit run by and for autistic people, working on policy and self-advocacy, with resources on health care, education, community living and accessibility. https://autisticadvocacy.org/
- Autistic Women & Nonbinary Network (AWN) (United States): A nonprofit focused on autistic women, girls, nonbinary and trans people, working from a neurodiversity and disability justice perspective. https://awnnetwork.org/
- National Autistic Society (United Kingdom): The UK's main autism charity, with advice across fourteen topic areas from diagnosis and employment to money and relationships, an online community, and an autism services directory. https://www.autism.org.uk/
- Reframing Autism (Australia): An autistic-led charity with a free Autistic Welcome Pack and a free Autism Essentials course, plus resources for people who are newly identified or still questioning. https://reframingautism.org.au/
- Autistica (United Kingdom): A UK autism research and campaigning charity focused on helping autistic people live long, healthy lives. https://www.autistica.org.uk/

### Getting assessed as an adult

Official information on how adult assessment works. Routes, waits and costs differ a great deal between countries, so start with the source for where you live.

- NHS: ADHD in adults (United Kingdom): How adult ADHD shows up and how assessment works on the NHS, starting with an appointment with a GP. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/
- NHS: Autism assessments (United Kingdom): What an NHS autism assessment involves and how to ask for one as an adult. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/autism/assessments/
- ADHD UK: Right to Choose (England): In England you have a legal right to choose who carries out your NHS ADHD or autism assessment, which can shorten long local waits. This guide explains how to ask your GP. https://adhduk.co.uk/right-to-choose/
- NICE guideline NG87: ADHD (United Kingdom): The clinical guideline UK services follow for diagnosing and managing ADHD, including in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87
- NICE guideline CG142: Autism in adults (United Kingdom): The clinical guideline for recognising, referring and diagnosing autism in adults in the UK. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142
- NIMH: ADHD (United States): Plain-language information on ADHD from the US National Institute of Mental Health. https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder-adhd
- NIMH: Autism spectrum disorder (United States): Plain-language information on autism from the US National Institute of Mental Health. https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/autism-spectrum-disorders-asd

### Self-screening questionnaires

Screeners can tell you whether an assessment is worth pursuing. They cannot diagnose you, and both sites below say so plainly. My article on what online ADHD and autism tests can tell you covers how to read the results.

- ADDA Adult ADHD Test (International): A short online self-screener based on the World Health Organization's Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS). ADDA describes it as a screening tool, not a diagnosis. https://add.org/adhd-test/
- Embrace Autism tests (International): Free online versions of widely used autism questionnaires, including the AQ, RAADS-R and the CAT-Q, which measures camouflaging. The site notes its content is not medical advice. https://embrace-autism.com/autism-tests/

### Finding a professional

Directories for finding clinicians, therapists and coaches who work with ADHD and autistic adults.

- CHADD Professional Directory (United States): A searchable directory of professionals and service providers working with ADHD. https://chadd.org/professional-directory/
- ADHD Coaches Organization (International): The professional association for ADHD coaches, with a searchable directory of coaches. https://www.adhdcoaches.org/
- Psychology Today therapist directory (United States): A large directory of therapists and counsellors, searchable by location, speciality and insurance. https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/therapists

### Peer support and body doubling

Talking to people who already understand saves a great deal of explaining. Virtual body doubling is included here because, for a lot of ADHD adults, other people's presence is what makes starting possible.

- Adult ADHD community (CHADD on HealthUnlocked) (International): A free online peer community for adults with ADHD, run with CHADD. https://healthunlocked.com/adult-ADHD
- Women with ADHD community (CHADD on HealthUnlocked) (International): A free online peer community for women with ADHD, run with CHADD. https://healthunlocked.com/adhd-women
- Focusmate (International): Virtual body doubling: short video sessions where you and another person each work on your own task. There is a free tier. https://www.focusmate.com/

### Work and reasonable adjustments

Your rights at work depend on where you live and who employs you. These are the official and expert sources, and they are a better guide than anything general I could write.

- Job Accommodation Network (JAN) (United States): Free, expert and confidential guidance on workplace accommodations, for employees and employers. https://askjan.org/
- JAN: ADHD accommodation ideas (United States): Practical workplace accommodation ideas for ADHD, organised by the difficulty they address. https://askjan.org/disabilities/Attention-Deficit-Hyperactivity-Disorder-AD-HD.cfm
- JAN: Autism accommodation ideas (United States): Practical workplace accommodation ideas for autistic employees. https://askjan.org/disabilities/Autism-Spectrum.cfm
- EEOC: Disability-related resources (United States): The US federal agency that enforces disability discrimination law at work. Its employment protections apply to employers with 15 or more employees. https://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc-disability-related-resources
- Acas: Reasonable adjustments at work (United Kingdom): What reasonable adjustments are and when the Equality Act 2010 requires an employer to make them. https://www.acas.org.uk/reasonable-adjustments
- Access to Work (England, Scotland and Wales): A UK government scheme that can fund support at work for disabled people and people with health conditions. Northern Ireland has a separate system. https://www.gov.uk/access-to-work

### Free debt and money advice

Not-for-profit services that will look at your situation for free. If anyone wants a fee to manage your debt, try one of these first.

- NFCC, National Foundation for Credit Counseling (United States): A network of non-profit credit counselling agencies that can help you work out a plan for your debt. https://www.nfcc.org/
- StepChange (United Kingdom): A UK debt charity offering free debt advice and fee-free debt management. https://www.stepchange.org/
- National Debtline (England and Wales): Free, confidential debt advice by phone, online chat or self-help tools. https://nationaldebtline.org/
- MABS, Money Advice and Budgeting Service (Ireland): Free, confidential help with money, debt and budgeting for people in Ireland. https://www.mabs.ie/en/
- National Debt Helpline (Australia): Free, confidential, not-for-profit financial counselling and step-by-step guides. https://ndh.org.au/
- Credit Counselling Canada (Canada): A national association of not-for-profit credit counselling agencies. https://creditcounsellingcanada.ca/

## Book: The ADHD Tax

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/
Subtitle: Stop Impulsive Spending, Forgotten Bills & Subscription Chaos
Series: Book 1 of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-10-21
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0FX3M9838

The ADHD tax is the money that leaves your account because of how your brain works rather than because of anything you chose to buy. Late fees on bills you had the money for. Subscriptions you meant to cancel. Things bought twice because the first one went missing.

This book is about stopping that, using systems that keep working on the weeks when you do not. It is the first book in the ADHD Money Mastery Series, and the one I recommend starting with if money is where ADHD costs you most.

### Who it's for

- You have paid late fees on bills you could actually afford.
- You keep finding subscriptions you forgot existed.
- You have tried several budgeting apps and none of them lasted.
- You have gone overdrawn despite fully intending to move money in time.
- You are tired of financial advice written for a brain that works differently from yours.

It is written for people diagnosed last month and for people who have managed executive dysfunction for decades. You do not need a diagnosis to use it.

### What's inside

The book works through the main places the ADHD tax comes from, and gives each one a system that does not depend on remembering or on willpower:

- Finding and cancelling the subscriptions that drain your account every month.
- Setting up autopay so late fees stop for good.
- Interrupting impulse purchases without trying to want things less.
- Paying off debt with an approach built around ADHD rather than around consistency.
- Building an emergency fund that grows without constant attention.
- Accountability systems that keep the whole thing running.

There is no shaming in it and no neurotypical budgeting template with ADHD stickers on it. The strategies are meant to be usable the same day you read them.

### Where it fits

The ADHD Tax diagnoses where the money goes. [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) is the guided 12-week version of putting a system in place, and [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/) goes deeper on clearing debt. If you want the short version first, the article on [what the ADHD tax actually costs](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/) covers the core idea, and the free [ADHD Tax Calculator](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/adhd-tax-calculator/) uses the same categories as the book's Chapter 1 worksheet.

### Common questions

### Is The ADHD Tax a workbook or a regular book?

It is a regular book, around 236 pages in print length on Amazon, with practical strategies throughout. If you want fill-in worksheets and a day-by-day structure, The ADHD Budget Workbook is the companion built for that.

### Do I need to be diagnosed with ADHD to use it?

No. The strategies are built around how ADHD affects money, and they work the same whether you have a formal diagnosis, suspect you have ADHD, or simply recognise yourself in the patterns.

### Should I read this before the other money books?

That is the order I would suggest, because it explains the patterns the other books build systems around. Each book in the series still stands alone, so starting elsewhere works too.

## Book: The ADHD Budget Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/
Subtitle: 90-Day Financial Reset for Adults with ADHD
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-11-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G1HH2M25

Most people with ADHD have tried budgeting and lasted about three weeks. This workbook is designed around that fact instead of pretending it will not happen again.

It is a guided 12-week program. Each day has one task that takes 15 to 30 minutes, so you are never deciding what to do next, and the structure expects you to miss days.

### Who it's for

- Traditional budgeting has failed you, usually by week three.
- Late fees, overdrafts and impulse spending keep happening anyway.
- You want out of the cycle of shame that money tends to produce.
- You need a system that works with how your brain runs, not one that asks you to become consistent first.

### What's inside

The program runs in four phases:

1. Weeks 1 to 3 stop the financial bleeding and set up the 3-Bucket System.
2. Weeks 4 to 6 automate everything and break impulsive spending patterns.
3. Weeks 7 to 9 build an emergency fund and start attacking debt.
4. Weeks 10 to 12 make the systems maintainable and begin building wealth.

Every strategy comes with a fill-in worksheet. There are visual progress trackers, checkpoints to mark progress, and flexibility built into the schedule for when life gets in the way. Week 10 is specifically about how to restart, because a plan that cannot survive a gap is not much use to an ADHD brain.

By the end, the aim is automated bill payments, a money system that does not lean on willpower, and an emergency fund that grows on its own.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) explains where the money goes and why. This workbook is the hands-on reset. Once the system exists, [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/) is the undated planner for keeping it running month after month. The article on [why ADHD brains overspend](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/) covers the spending side in more depth.

### Common questions

### What happens if I miss a day or a week?

You pick up where you left off. The workbook is built on the assumption that you will miss days, and week 10 is devoted to restarting after you have fallen off.

### How much time does it take each day?

Each daily task is designed to take 15 to 30 minutes. On a bad day the guidance is to do a single task and stop.

### Do I need spreadsheets or budgeting software?

No. Everything happens in the workbook itself, with worksheets for each step and no complicated spreadsheets to maintain.

## Book: The ADHD Side Hustle

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-side-hustle/
Subtitle: Turn Your Hyperfocus Into Extra Income Without Burning Out
Series: Book 3 of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2025-11-15
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G2HRQTWJ

At some point, cutting costs stops being enough and the only remaining lever is earning more. Most side hustle advice then tells you to stay focused and be consistent, which is the advice least likely to work for an ADHD brain.

This book is about building extra income around the way ADHD actually behaves: in bursts, driven by interest, with variable energy. It is the third book in the ADHD Money Mastery Series.

### Who it's for

Adults with ADHD who are tired of jobs that do not fit how they work. People who have got their spending under control and still cannot earn enough for budgeting to matter. Anyone who has started several businesses and finished none of them. Freelancers who need systems that hold up on bad days.

### What's inside

The book treats hyperfocus, pattern recognition and tolerance for risk as advantages, then deals honestly with the costs that come with them. It covers:

- 25 side hustles rated for how well they suit an ADHD brain, including which ones to avoid.
- The 48-Hour Business Launch Challenge, for starting without overthinking.
- Getting your first client without feeling like a salesperson.
- The 3-Bucket Business Money System.
- Time management for variable energy levels.
- Using AI to cover the tasks ADHD makes hardest.
- The 90-Day Focus Rule, for breaking the cycle of starting and quitting.
- How to tell when to quit and when to pivot.
- Simplified legal and tax basics.

It includes templates: a launch checklist, a service pricing calculator, email and proposal templates, a monthly business review, and a tax deduction tracking sheet. The roadmap runs from a first $100 through $500 and $1,000.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) and [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) deal with money going out. This book is about money coming in. The article on [hyperfocus without the crash](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/) covers the burnout side of working in bursts.

### Common questions

### Do I need a business idea before reading it?

No. The book rates 25 side hustles for ADHD compatibility specifically so you can choose one that suits how you work, rather than starting from an idea and hoping it fits.

### How does it deal with shiny object syndrome?

Directly. The 90-Day Focus Rule is about channelling the urge to start new things instead of trying to eliminate it, and there is guidance on telling a genuine pivot from another abandoned project.

### Is it only for people starting a business?

It is also written for existing freelancers who need better systems for time, clients and money, particularly ones that survive low-energy weeks.

## Book: The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/
Subtitle: A Step-by-Step Workbook to Help You Pay Off Debt, Build Momentum, and Create Financial Freedom
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2026-08-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK1RYSW

Every debt plan most of us have quit relied on exactly what ADHD makes hardest: remembering due dates, resisting the pull of spending, feeling consequences that are months away, and doing a boring task the same way for years.

This workbook does not ask your brain to change. It replaces memory with autopilot, puts visible wins on a weekly schedule, and gives you restart pages for the times you disappear.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD carrying debt they have tried and failed to clear, whether that is credit cards, buy-now-pay-later accounts, medical bills, or all of them at once. It is written for the reality of a pile of unopened post and plans that always start on Monday.

### What's inside

It is a six-month workbook. You will:

- Face every debt in one sitting with the "Envelope Amnesty", where estimates are allowed and shame is not required.
- Choose a payoff method in two minutes with a short quiz: snowball, avalanche, or the ADHD Hybrid.
- Put every payment on autopilot so late fees stop from the first day.
- Run 10-minute weekly check-ins designed to survive bad weeks.
- Colour in debt thermometers that make progress hard to ignore.
- Use Missed-Payment and Restart pages when life gets in the way.

There are no spreadsheets to maintain and no 47-category budgets. The system assumes you will vanish for three weeks at some point and keeps working when you come back.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) introduces the patterns behind ADHD money problems, including debt. This workbook is the dedicated tool for paying debt down. Once you are through it, [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/) keeps the rest of your money running. The article on [why payoff plans keep failing](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/) explains the thinking behind the approach.

### Common questions

### Snowball or avalanche: which does the workbook use?

You choose. A short quiz at the start helps you pick between the snowball method, the avalanche method, or the ADHD Hybrid, depending on what will keep you going.

### What if I miss a payment or abandon the workbook for a while?

The workbook expects that. There is a Missed-Payment page and a Restart page specifically for coming back after a gap, without starting from zero.

### How long does it take?

The workbook is structured around six months, with a 10-minute check-in each week.

## Book: The ADHD Budget Planner

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-planner/
Subtitle: The Undated 12-Month Money Management System for Adults with ADHD
Series: Part of The ADHD Money Mastery Series
Published: 2026-08-08
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK4TZGF

Dated planners have a built-in failure point: the first skipped week. For an ADHD brain that week always arrives, and then the planner goes in a drawer with the guilt attached.

This one is undated. You name the months yourself, you can start in any of them, and missing one does not break anything.

### Who it's for

Adults with ADHD who have abandoned planners before and want a money system that waits for them when they come back. It also suits anyone who has built a budget system and needs somewhere to keep it running year after year.

### What's inside

It opens with a one-hour Setup section, which does most of the heavy lifting:

- A Bills Master List that gets every due date out of your head and onto paper.
- The Subscription Hunt, for finding charges you forgot about and reclaiming that money.
- The Autopilot Checklist, covering autopay, moved due dates and payment confirmations.

Then there are twelve identical undated months. Each has a one-page Money Map of the month's budget, a bill due-date tracker, four 10-minute weekly check-ins, an ADHD Tax log that records late fees, impulse buys and forgotten subscriptions, and a month review. Quarterly pit stops use a one-change rule to stop you rebuilding the whole system instead of using it.

For the hard moments there is a Missed-Payment page that scripts the call asking for a fee to be waived, a Restart page for when you find the planner after weeks away, and colourable progress trackers.

### Where it fits

The planner is the long-term home for a system. [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-budget-workbook/) is the guided 90-day reset that builds it. [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-debt-payoff-workbook/) handles debt specifically, and [The ADHD Tax](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-tax/) explains the patterns all of it is designed around.

### Common questions

### Why is the planner undated?

Because the skipped week is where dated planners fail. Undated months mean you can start any time, miss a month, and continue without blank pages reminding you of the gap.

### How long does setup take?

The Setup section is designed to take about an hour. After that, each week needs a 10-minute check-in.

### Do I need the Budget Workbook first?

No, the planner works on its own. The workbook is useful if you want a guided program to build the system before you start maintaining it in the planner.

## Book: The ADHD Overthinking Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/
Subtitle: Break Free from Mental Loops, Quiet Intrusive Thoughts, and Stop Spiraling — Even When Your Brain Won't Shut Up
Series: Book 1 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2025-12-31
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDGK3RLK

It is two in the morning and your brain is replaying a conversation from three days ago. You are tired, you know none of this matters at this hour, and the loop keeps running anyway.

The usual advice, to breathe or think positively or journal it out, tends to fall apart the moment you are actually inside the spiral. This book is a set of fast interventions for that moment, written for ADHD brains. It is the first book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD who gets caught in mental loops: replaying conversations, spiralling over what someone meant, lying awake with racing thoughts. It is especially aimed at the spirals that hit ADHD brains hardest, including rejection sensitivity, money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and nighttime overthinking.

### What's inside

The chapters are short and the tools are meant to be used in the moment:

- The 90-Second Interrupt, for breaking a loop before it takes over your day.
- The 5-Minute Grounding Protocol, for when overstimulation is pushing you toward shutdown.
- How to handle intrusive thoughts without fighting them or feeding them.
- How to make decisions without needing perfect certainty first.
- Specific approaches for rejection sensitive dysphoria, money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and sleepless nights.
- A prevention system that does not require a perfect morning routine.

The goal is not to stop spiralling forever. It is to catch rumination earlier, recover faster, and treat yourself more kindly along the way.

### Where it fits

The Reset Series takes one stuck pattern per book. [The ADHD Eating Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/) covers meal paralysis and [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) covers analysis paralysis. For more on the nighttime version of this problem, read [the 2 a.m. spiral](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/), and for the emotional side, [rejection sensitive dysphoria](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/rejection-sensitive-dysphoria/).

### Common questions

### How long is the book?

It is short on purpose, around 69 pages in print length on Amazon, with brief chapters you can use when your attention is limited.

### Does it cover rejection sensitive dysphoria?

Yes. RSD is one of the specific spirals the book addresses, alongside money anxiety, productivity guilt, relationship overthinking and nighttime overthinking.

### Is it about meditation?

No. The tools are quick, practical interrupts rather than meditation practices or long routines.

## Book: The ADHD Eating Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/
Subtitle: End Meal Paralysis, Stop Forgetting to Eat, and Build Food Habits Your ADHD Brain Will Actually Keep
Series: Book 2 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2025-12-31
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDH6R4DL

It is four in the afternoon and you have just realised you have not eaten. Not because you were skipping meals. You forgot. Now you are standing at the fridge, starving and irritable, unable to choose anything.

ADHD changes how you process hunger, time, decisions and reward, which is why generic food advice rarely sticks. This book has no meal plans and no diets. It is a set of tools for eating consistently, even imperfectly. It is the second book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

- You forget to eat, then crash hard when you finally remember.
- You spend twenty minutes deciding what to eat and end up with nothing.
- You eat the same safe foods on repeat because deciding is exhausting.
- You have tried meal planning and abandoned it by Wednesday.
- You sometimes eat crackers for dinner and feel terrible about it.

### What's inside

- The "Just Eat Something" Protocol, which breaks meal paralysis in about 90 seconds.
- The Decision Funnel, for ending "what should I eat?" spirals.
- The Cooking Activation System, for days when cooking feels impossible.
- How to interrupt dopamine-driven eating without shame or restriction.
- How to stop forgetting to eat, and what to do when you forget anyway.
- Strategies for grocery shopping, eating with other people, and emotional eating.

The aim is eating consistently, even if it is the same thing every day.

### Where it fits

This is one book in the Reset Series, which takes on one stuck pattern at a time. [The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) covers mental loops and [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) covers analysis paralysis, which overlaps heavily with food decisions. The article on [meal paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-meal-paralysis-forgetting-to-eat/) is a good place to start.

### Common questions

### Is this a diet book?

No. There are no diets and no meal plans. It is about the executive function side of eating: remembering, deciding and getting started.

### Is it okay to eat the same foods every day?

The book treats repetitive safe foods as a reasonable strategy rather than a failure. For specific nutritional questions, a doctor or dietitian is the right person to ask.

### Does it help with forgetting to eat?

Yes, that is one of its main subjects, along with what to do when you have already forgotten and are past the point of making good decisions.

## Book: The ADHD Decision Reset

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/
Subtitle: Break Analysis Paralysis, Make Choices Faster, and Stop Overthinking Everything
Series: Book 3 of The ADHD Reset Series
Published: 2026-01-01
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDMWFDZ7

Everyone else at the table has ordered. You have been looking at the menu for ten minutes and still cannot decide. It is rarely about the food.

ADHD changes how decisions get processed, which is why ordinary choices can feel overwhelming and why "just pick one" does not help. This book gives you fixed protocols that turn decisions into something you can finish in two to ten minutes. It is the third book in the ADHD Reset Series.

### Who it's for

Anyone with ADHD who has spent twenty minutes choosing a meal, weeks researching a purchase without buying, or years "figuring out" a career. Also anyone who freezes in front of a to-do list because every item looks equally urgent.

### What's inside

The core of the book is three protocols matched to the size of the decision:

- The 2-Minute Decision Protocol for everyday choices like what to eat, wear or do.
- The 5-Minute Decision Protocol for medium decisions such as purchases and plans.
- The 10-Minute Decision Protocol for large life choices about work and relationships.

Around those sit the Emergency Decision Interrupt for when you are frozen, a method for removing most routine daily decisions altogether, and a "good enough" standard for perfectionism paralysis. It works through specific traps: food, shopping, prioritising tasks, career and life decisions, and avoiding difficult conversations.

The goal is not to turn you into a decisive person. It is to make decisions fast enough to get on with your life.

### Where it fits

[The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) covers rumination more broadly, and [The ADHD Eating Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-eating-reset/) deals with the food version of this problem. The articles on [decision paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-decision-paralysis/) and [task paralysis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-task-paralysis/) go deeper on why choosing is so hard.

### Common questions

### Does it help with big decisions or only small ones?

Both. There is a separate protocol for large life decisions about career and relationships, as well as the shorter ones for everyday and medium choices.

### What is the "good enough" standard?

It is the book's approach to perfectionism paralysis: choosing a level of quality that is sufficient instead of searching for the best possible option.

### Is decision paralysis an ADHD thing?

Difficulty making decisions is commonly reported by adults with ADHD and is linked to executive function. It also overlaps with anxiety, so if indecision is part of broader, persistent worry, it is worth discussing with a professional.

## Book: The ADHD Burnout Recovery Guide

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-burnout-recovery/
Subtitle: Triage, Recovery, and Prevention for the Brain You Actually Have
Series: Standalone guide
Published: 2026-01-01
Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GDLRFXQ3

Standard burnout advice is rest, boundaries and self-care. It assumes a brain with steady energy and reliable executive function, which ADHD brains do not have. That is why the advice keeps failing.

This book treats ADHD burnout as a high-cost system that broke from running too long without enough maintenance, and gives you protocols built for that.

### Who it's for

- You have been called lazy or told you were not applying yourself for as long as you can remember.
- You have crashed, recovered, and crashed again, and you are tired of the cycle.
- Standard burnout advice reads as though it was written for someone else.
- You want something specific and honest about how your brain works.

### What's inside

- A five-minute triage you can do in bed when you are already crashing.
- Yellow, orange and red burnout zones, and what to do at each level.
- Recovery protocols for the three things that fail in every ADHD burnout: motivation, executive function and masking.
- The four patterns that produce ADHD burnout: overcommitment, perfectionism, understimulation and hyperfocus crashes, with ways to interrupt each.
- Energy management in place of time management.
- Prevention systems that keep working once willpower runs out.

The book is laid out for how you will actually arrive at it. If you are crashing right now, Chapter 4 has the five-minute triage. If you are noticing warning signs, start at Chapter 2. If you have recovered once and are crashing again, the middle of the book covers the patterns behind the cycle.

### Where it fits

This is a standalone book. If you are AuDHD, [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/) covers autistic burnout alongside masking. The article on [autistic burnout, ADHD burnout and depression](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-burnout-vs-adhd-burnout-vs-depression/) explains how to tell them apart, and [hyperfocus without the crash](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/) covers one of the four patterns.

### Common questions

### Where should I start if I am burnt out right now?

Chapter 4, which is a five-minute triage designed to be done in bed. The rest can wait until you have some capacity back.

### Is ADHD burnout the same as depression?

No, although they can overlap and occur together. If you have persistent low mood, have lost interest in things you used to enjoy, or are having thoughts of harming yourself, please speak to a doctor. This book is not a substitute for that.

### Does it cover masking?

Yes. Masking is one of the three failures the recovery protocols address, along with motivation and executive function.

## Article: ADHD or autism? How to tell them apart in adults

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-vs-autism-adults/
Published: 2026-10-22
Summary: ADHD and autism overlap more than most descriptions admit. The differences that actually help adults tell which is which, and why it is often both.

Most adults who start looking into this have already noticed the problem. They read a description of ADHD and recognise themselves. Then they read a description of autism and recognise themselves there too. The lists overlap enough that recognising yourself in one does not rule out the other.

That is not a failure of attention on your part. The two conditions share a great deal, they frequently occur together, and some of the clearest differences are about why a behaviour happens rather than what it looks like.

### Key takeaways

- The same behaviour often has a different cause in ADHD than in autism, and the cause is what distinguishes them.
- ADHD tends toward novelty and variety; autism tends toward predictability and depth.
- Social difficulty differs: missing the timing versus missing the unwritten rules.
- Sensory differences and a need for sameness point more toward autism; impulsivity and time blindness point more toward ADHD.
- Having both is common, which is why so many people see themselves in both lists.

### The same behaviour, different reason

This is the most useful lens I have found, and it is the one most checklists leave out.

Take interrupting people. With ADHD it is usually impulsivity: the thought will evaporate if it is not said now, so it comes out. With autism it is more often about conversational timing, not reading the subtle cues that mark a gap, or being so engaged with the topic that the social choreography fades.

Take being overwhelmed in a supermarket. With ADHD that is often too many competing things to attend to, with attention bouncing between them. With autism it is more often the sensory load itself: the lighting, the noise, the number of choices on the shelf.

Take rigidity around plans. An autistic person may need the plan because a change is genuinely costly to process. Someone with ADHD may cling to a plan because they know that without it the day will evaporate, or may abandon it entirely because the plan has become boring.

Take losing track of time. With ADHD it tends to be a weak felt sense of time passing. With autism it is more often that a deep interest has absorbed everything, and the clock was never in view.

The outward behaviour is the same. The mechanism is not.

> Checklists compare behaviours. The two conditions are easier to separate by asking what the behaviour is doing for you.

### Where they pull in opposite directions

A few patterns tend to separate more cleanly.

Novelty versus sameness is the big one. ADHD is drawn toward new, interesting and stimulating things, and finds repetition genuinely hard to tolerate. Autism tends toward predictability, familiar routines, the same meal, the same route. Someone who is both will feel the contradiction constantly, which is its own clue.

Social difficulty differs in texture. Many autistic adults describe missing the unwritten rules: not knowing how long to hold eye contact, or how direct is too direct, and learning those things explicitly rather than absorbing them. Many ADHD adults describe knowing the rules perfectly and breaking them anyway, through interrupting, over-talking, or forgetting to reply for three weeks.

Sensory experience is weighted toward autism. Sensory sensitivity exists in ADHD too, but a lifelong, pervasive pattern of sensory needs shaping your clothing, food and environment points more strongly toward autism.

Interests differ in shape. ADHD interest is often intense and short-lived: a new hobby every few months, with the equipment from the last three in a cupboard. Autistic special interests tend to be deep and durable, sometimes lifelong, and are a reliable source of regulation rather than novelty.

Impulsivity and time blindness are more characteristic of ADHD. Need for routine, difficulty with transitions and distress at unexpected change are more characteristic of autism.

### Why so many people see both

Because for a lot of people, both apply.

The two co-occur often enough that the combination has its own informal name, AuDHD, and diagnostic rules in several countries used to prohibit recording both, which left many adults with half an explanation. If you recognise yourself in both descriptions and the contradictions feel familiar, that is worth taking seriously rather than treating as confusion.

There is also a masking problem. An autistic adult who learned to perform social behaviour very well may look ADHD from outside, because what shows is the disorganisation rather than the social effort. And someone with ADHD who built heavy routines to compensate can look autistic, because what shows is the rigidity.

### What this is not

This is not a diagnostic tool, and I am not a clinician. The distinctions above are the ones that helped me understand my own experience and the ones I see other late-identified adults find useful. They are not criteria.

A clinician separating these will look at developmental history, how things presented in childhood, how difficulties show up across different settings, and what else might explain them. That is a different process from recognising yourself in a description, and it is worth doing if you want an answer you can act on.

### What to do with the question

If you are trying to work out which, the most useful preparation is to collect examples rather than labels. For each thing you struggle with, write down what actually happens and what it feels like from inside. Did you interrupt because you would lose the thought, or because you did not notice the pause? Is the supermarket hard because of the noise or because of the choices?

That detail is what a good assessment works from, and it is the part you cannot reconstruct in the room. The article on [getting assessed as an adult](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adult-adhd-autism-assessment/) covers the rest of the preparation.

### Common questions

### Can you have both ADHD and autism?

Yes, and it is common. The informal term for it is AuDHD. Diagnostic rules in several countries once prevented clinicians from recording both, so many adults were given whichever was noticed first. Those rules have changed, although practice has not caught up everywhere.

### What is the main difference between ADHD and autism?

In broad terms, ADHD centres on attention, impulsivity and the executive functions that organise behaviour, while autism centres on social communication, sensory processing and a need for predictability. In practice the clearest difference is often why a given behaviour happens rather than what it looks like.

### Can ADHD be mistaken for autism?

Yes, in both directions. Someone with ADHD who built heavy routines to compensate can appear rigid, and an autistic adult who masks well can appear simply disorganised. Social difficulties, sensory sensitivity and trouble with focus occur in both, which is why assessment relies on developmental history rather than a symptom list alone.

### Which should I get assessed for first?

That is usually a question for the clinician rather than something to decide in advance. Describe everything you experience rather than steering toward one label, because the overlap is exactly what they are trained to untangle. If you have already been diagnosed with one and the strategies only partly work, the other is worth raising.

### Where should I start reading?

If the contradictions sound familiar, start with [AuDHD](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/audhd-autistic-and-adhd/). If one side clearly fits better, [the first year after an ADHD diagnosis](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/) and [finding out you are autistic](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/) cover what tends to come next.

## Article: ADHD or anxiety? Which came first, and why it matters

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-vs-anxiety/
Published: 2026-10-22
Summary: ADHD and anxiety look alike and often occur together. The questions that help separate them, and why treating anxiety alone sometimes only half works.

A great many late-diagnosed adults have the same story. They were treated for anxiety first, sometimes for years. The treatment helped, genuinely, but only to a point. Something underneath never shifted, and nobody could say what it was.

Anxiety and ADHD produce a lot of the same surface: trouble concentrating, restlessness, a racing mind, difficulty sleeping, a constant sense of being behind. Telling them apart matters because the thing you treat determines whether the rest of it moves.

### Key takeaways

- Both can wreck concentration, so the symptom itself does not separate them.
- A useful question is whether focus is difficult even on calm, good days.
- Another is whether the difficulty goes back to childhood, before there was much to be anxious about.
- Anxiety is frequently a consequence of undiagnosed ADHD rather than a separate problem.
- They co-occur often, so this is about what to treat rather than choosing one.

### Why they look so similar

Start with concentration. Anxiety occupies working memory with worry, which leaves less available for the task in front of you. ADHD affects the attention system directly. From the outside, and often from the inside, both feel like being unable to think straight.

Restlessness looks alike too. Anxious restlessness is driven by threat: the body is prepared for something. ADHD restlessness is driven by understimulation: the body is looking for input. Both produce fidgeting, pacing, and an inability to sit through a film.

Sleep is similar in both. Anxiety keeps you awake with worry; ADHD keeps you awake with a mind that will not stop generating material and an evening that finally belongs to you.

And avoidance looks identical. Anxious avoidance is about the feared outcome. ADHD avoidance is usually about the wall between deciding to start and starting. Both end with the task not done and a growing sense of dread about it.

### Questions that help separate them

None of these is a test. They are the questions I have found most useful for describing the difference accurately to someone qualified.

**Is it hard to focus on a calm, good day?** This is the most discriminating one. Anxiety tends to wreck focus when worry is active. If your attention is just as unreliable on a relaxed Saturday with nothing to worry about, that points more toward ADHD.

**How far back does it go?** ADHD is present from early in life. If attention, organisation and finishing things were already difficult in primary school, before there was much to be anxious about, that matters. School reports are genuinely useful here.

**Does it happen everywhere?** ADHD difficulties tend to show up across most settings. Anxiety is more often tied to particular situations, even if those situations are broad.

**What is the thought doing?** Anxious rumination usually has content: a specific fear, a scenario, a consequence. The ADHD version is often less about dread and more about volume, with the mind generating ideas, tangents and replays of social moments without a central fear.

**What happened when anxiety was treated?** If therapy or medication reduced the worry but left the lateness, the unfinished projects, the lost keys and the inability to start, that remainder is worth investigating rather than accepting.

> Anxiety treatment that works on the worry and leaves everything else untouched is telling you something useful.

### Anxiety as a consequence

This is the part I wish someone had said to me earlier.

If you grow up with undiagnosed ADHD, you accumulate evidence that you are unreliable. Deadlines missed, things forgotten, people let down, work that was good when it finally arrived and often arrived late. After enough years of that, a certain amount of anxiety is a rational response to your own track record. You become anxious because experience taught you that things go wrong and you cannot predict when.

That kind of anxiety is real, and it responds partially to anxiety treatment. What it responds to more completely is addressing the thing generating the evidence. Several people I have spoken to described their anxiety dropping substantially once their ADHD was treated and their systems stopped collapsing, not because the anxiety was fake, but because its source was reduced.

The reverse is also possible. Chronic anxiety genuinely impairs attention, and treating it can resolve focus problems entirely. Which is why this is a question for assessment rather than for self-diagnosis.

### When it is both

Often it is. Anxiety is one of the most commonly reported co-occurring conditions in adults with ADHD, and having one does not protect you from the other.

When both are present, the practical question is sequencing, and that is a conversation with a clinician. Some people need the anxiety brought down before anything else is workable. Others find that the ADHD support is what makes the anxiety manageable. There is no single right order, and anyone who tells you there is does not know your situation.

### What to do

Write down examples rather than adjectives, and include the calm days. "I could not start the report on a quiet Sunday with no deadline pressure and nothing else on" is far more useful to a clinician than "I have trouble focusing".

Then take it to someone qualified. If you have been treated for anxiety and a stubborn remainder never shifted, say that explicitly. It is one of the more common routes to a late ADHD diagnosis, and it is the kind of detail that gets missed unless you raise it.

### Common questions

### Can ADHD be misdiagnosed as anxiety?

It commonly is, particularly in adults who were not identified as children. The surface symptoms overlap heavily, and anxiety is the more familiar explanation. Many late-diagnosed adults report being treated for anxiety for years before ADHD was considered.

### How do I know if it is ADHD or anxiety?

The most useful questions are whether focus is difficult even on calm days, whether the difficulties go back to childhood, and whether they show up across most settings rather than specific ones. These are not diagnostic, and only an assessment that considers your developmental history can answer it properly.

### Can anxiety cause ADHD symptoms?

Anxiety can genuinely impair attention, working memory and sleep, which produces something that looks a lot like ADHD. The distinguishing feature is usually that anxiety-driven difficulty tracks with how anxious you are, while ADHD difficulty persists regardless.

### Does treating ADHD help anxiety?

For some people it does, particularly when the anxiety grew out of years of things going wrong. For others the anxiety is separate and needs its own treatment. Both are common. This is a question for a prescriber or therapist who knows your history rather than something to decide from an article.

### Where should I start?
