If the racing mind is the worst part, [the 2 a.m. spiral](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-overthinking-2am-spiral/) covers it in more depth, and [The ADHD Overthinking Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-overthinking-reset/) has tools for the moment itself. If you want to pursue assessment, [how to get assessed as an adult](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adult-adhd-autism-assessment/) explains the process.

## Article: Autistic meltdown or panic attack? Telling them apart

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-meltdown-vs-panic-attack/
Published: 2026-10-22
Summary: Meltdowns and panic attacks can look alike from outside and need different responses. What distinguishes them, and what helps during each.

From outside they can look the same: someone distressed, crying, struggling to speak, needing to get out of the room. The responses that help are close to opposite, which is why the distinction is worth understanding even though it is not always clean.

I want to be careful here. Panic attacks are a clinical matter, autistic people experience them at least as often as anyone else, and the two can happen in the same episode. What follows is how the experiences tend to differ, not a way to diagnose yourself.

### Key takeaways

- Meltdowns are usually driven by accumulated overload; panic attacks are usually driven by fear.
- Overload tends to build over hours or days, while panic often arrives abruptly.
- Panic attacks typically carry strong physical fear symptoms and a sense of dread or danger.
- Reassurance helps panic; reducing sensory input helps a meltdown.
- They can occur together, and a clinician is the right person to untangle it.

### What tends to drive each

A meltdown is generally the end of a load problem. Sensory input, social effort, masking, uncertainty and demands accumulate across hours or days until there is no capacity left, and control of your responses goes. The final trigger is often trivial, which is one of the recognisable features: a dropped glass or a changed plan sets off something wildly out of proportion to it, because the real cause was everything that came before.

A panic attack is generally a fear response. The body's alarm system fires, often without a proportionate external cause, and produces intense physical symptoms: racing heart, shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, sweating, and frequently a sense of dread or a conviction that something terrible is happening.

That difference in driver is the most useful thing to hold onto. One is a system that has run out of capacity. The other is a system that has sounded an alarm.

### Differences people describe

**The build.** Meltdowns usually have a run-up, even if you did not notice it: rising irritability, sounds getting sharper, stimming increasing, an urge to leave. Panic attacks more often arrive suddenly, sometimes with no warning at all.

**The physical signature.** The cardiac and respiratory symptoms, the feeling of not being able to breathe, and the fear of dying or losing control are characteristic of panic. Meltdowns can involve physical distress, but the specific terror-plus-heart-racing combination is more typical of panic.

**What is in your head.** During panic there is usually fear with content: something bad is happening or about to. During a meltdown people more often describe being past thought entirely, flooded, unable to process language, with no specific fear attached.

**What preceded it.** If you can trace a day or a week of accumulating demand, that points toward overload. If it came out of a calm afternoon, that points more toward panic.

**What helps.** This is the most practical difference. Panic generally responds to grounding, slowed breathing and reassurance that you are safe. A meltdown generally does not respond to reassurance, and talking at someone in one usually makes it worse. What helps is less: less noise, less light, fewer people, fewer words.

> With panic, being talked to calmly often helps. With a meltdown, being talked to at all is usually more input than the system can take.

I would treat the often repeated claim that meltdowns last longer than panic attacks with some caution. Both vary enormously, and duration is a weak way to tell them apart compared with what caused the episode and what helps during it.

### They are not mutually exclusive

Plenty of autistic people experience both, sometimes close together. Sensory overload is frightening, and fear is an entirely reasonable response to feeling your control slipping in public. An episode can begin as overload and become panic, or the reverse.

Autistic adults also experience anxiety disorders at high rates, which is worth knowing if you are trying to make sense of recurring episodes. The fact that you are autistic does not mean every episode is a meltdown.

### What to do during each

If it looks like overload, reduce input. Leave if you can. Headphones, a quiet room, a car, a dim space. Fewer words from anyone present. Recovery usually takes longer than the episode and may include a headache, exhaustion or emotional flatness for a day or more.

If it looks like panic, grounding tends to help: slower breathing, naming things you can see, feeling something solid, and a reminder that the feeling will pass. Panic attacks are intensely unpleasant and generally not dangerous, though that is much easier to hold onto when someone else says it.

If you are supporting someone and cannot tell which it is, the safest default is to reduce the input, stay nearby, say very little, avoid touching them unless you know they want it, and make sure they are safe. That is unlikely to make either worse.

### When to involve a professional

If you are having recurring episodes of either kind, or if fear of the next one is shaping where you go and what you do, that is worth raising with a doctor. Panic disorder is treatable, and treatment works a good deal better than endurance.

If any episode involves thoughts of harming yourself, please contact a crisis line or emergency services. The [resources directory](https://jmstruijk.com/resources/#crisis) lists free crisis support by country.

### Common questions

### What is the difference between an autistic meltdown and a panic attack?

A meltdown is generally a response to accumulated sensory, social or emotional overload, while a panic attack is generally a fear response with strong physical symptoms such as a racing heart and shortness of breath. They can look similar from outside, and the clearest difference is usually what caused the episode and what helps during it.

### Can autistic people have panic attacks?

Yes. Being autistic does not make panic attacks less likely, and anxiety disorders are commonly reported among autistic adults. An episode can also begin as overload and develop into panic.

### How can I tell which one I am having?

Afterwards, look at what preceded it. A day or week of accumulating demand points toward overload. A sudden onset from a calm state with intense physical fear symptoms points toward panic. What helped is also informative: reassurance tends to help panic, while reducing input tends to help a meltdown.

### Does breathing exercises help a meltdown?

Often not, and being coached through breathing can add demand at a moment when processing language is already hard. Grounding and breathing are more associated with panic. For a meltdown, reducing sensory input and giving space tends to help more.

### What should I do afterwards?

Treat recovery as part of the event rather than a separate thing. Rest, low input, and no analysis until you have capacity again. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-autistic-workbook/) covers reading your energy before it reaches zero, which is where most of the prevention lives.

## Article: Inattentive ADHD in adults: the quiet presentation

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/inattentive-adhd-adults/
Published: 2026-10-22
Summary: Inattentive ADHD has no visible hyperactivity, which is why so many adults reach their thirties without it being noticed. How it actually shows up.

The hyperactivity is there. It just went inward.

That is the sentence that landed hardest for me when I was working out what had been going on. The picture of ADHD most of us grew up with was a boy who could not stay in his seat. If you were the quiet one staring out of the window, finishing the work eventually, well-behaved and slightly absent, nobody looked any further.

Inattentive ADHD is the presentation without visible hyperactivity. It is extremely easy to miss, and a large share of adults identified late fall into it.

### Key takeaways

- The inattentive presentation involves attention and executive function without obvious outward hyperactivity.
- Restlessness is often internal: a mind that will not settle rather than a body that will not sit.
- It is missed in childhood because it disrupts nobody except the person experiencing it.
- Academic ability frequently hides it until demands outgrow compensation.
- It is the same condition as other presentations and is diagnosed the same way.

### What it actually looks like

Forget the window-staring image for a moment. In adult life it tends to show up as a cluster of things that do not obviously belong together until you have the frame.

Reading a page four times and retaining none of it. Hearing someone say your name and realising you have no idea what the last two sentences were about, even though you were trying.

Losing things constantly, and the specific exhaustion of knowing you will lose the next thing too.

Starting tasks and leaving them at ninety percent. The email drafted and unsent, the washing in the machine for two days, the form filled in and not submitted.

Underestimating how long everything takes, and the lateness that follows.

Mental clutter: forty open loops, none of them closed, all of them surfacing at once at three in the morning.

And the one that surprises people, because it does not sound like inattention at all: a mind that will not quieten. Internal restlessness is still restlessness. Many adults with the inattentive presentation describe constant mental motion, which is why the hyperactive label never seemed to fit even though something was clearly running too fast.

> Inattentive ADHD is not an attention shortage. It is attention that will not stay where you point it.

### Why it gets missed

It disrupts nobody. A child who cannot sit still interrupts a classroom and gets referred. A child who drifts quietly gets described as dreamy, or careless, or not applying themselves, and the school moves on.

Academic ability covers it for a long time. If you are bright enough to produce good work in a panic the night before, the system records the outcome rather than the method. The difficulty only becomes visible when the volume of work outgrows what a last-minute sprint can absorb, which for many people is university, a first demanding job, or parenthood.

Compensation hides the rest. Lists, alarms, overpreparation, arriving an hour early because you cannot judge time, rereading everything three times. Those strategies work, at a cost nobody can see, and the cost is why so many people arrive at an assessment exhausted rather than obviously impaired.

And girls and women were missed at far higher rates, partly because the inattentive presentation is more commonly recognised in them and partly because the diagnostic picture in use was built from observations of boys.

### It is the same condition

Worth saying plainly, because the old name confuses people. You will still see "ADD" used for the inattentive presentation. Current diagnostic practice treats it as one condition with different presentations, so a clinician would describe it as ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.

That matters practically. It is assessed the same way, the same treatment options are on the table, and the same workplace adjustments apply. Having no visible hyperactivity does not make it a milder condition, and plenty of people with this presentation are substantially affected by it.

Presentations can also shift. Many adults describe hyperactivity that was more visible in childhood and became internal with age.

### What helps

The strategies are much the same as for ADHD generally, with a couple of emphases.

External structure matters more than usual, because nothing about this presentation announces itself. If a task is not written down somewhere you will physically see it, it does not exist. Visible lists, visible clocks, alarms for leaving rather than for the event.

Closing loops is the specific relief. Mental clutter is the defining experience here, and the fix is not better memory but fewer open items: finish small things immediately, write the rest down, and formally abandon what you are never going to do.

Body doubling works particularly well for the start problem, which tends to be where this presentation loses most of its time.

And lower the volume of self-criticism where you can. The inattentive presentation comes with decades of being called careless by people who could not see the effort. That accumulates, and it makes every system harder to sustain.

### Common questions

### What is inattentive ADHD?

It is the presentation of ADHD characterised by difficulties with attention, organisation, working memory and follow-through, without prominent outward hyperactivity. It is sometimes still called ADD, though current practice treats it as one of the presentations of ADHD rather than a separate condition.

### Is inattentive ADHD less severe?

No. Visible hyperactivity is not a measure of how much a condition affects someone's life. Many adults with this presentation are substantially affected, and the lack of outward signs is a common reason they went unidentified for decades.

### Can you have inattentive ADHD and still be restless?

Yes, and many people describe exactly that. Restlessness is often internal: a mind in constant motion rather than a body that cannot stay seated. That is one reason the hyperactive label never seemed to fit, even when something clearly was.

### Why was my inattentive ADHD missed as a child?

Mostly because it disrupts nobody else. Quiet drifting gets interpreted as daydreaming or carelessness rather than investigated, and academic ability often covers the difficulty until demands grow. Girls were missed at particularly high rates.

### What should I do if this describes me?

Collect concrete examples of how it affects you now and what you remember of childhood, then speak to a doctor about assessment. [How to get assessed as an adult](https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adult-adhd-autism-assessment/) covers the process, and [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://jmstruijk.com/books/late-diagnosed-adhd-workbook/) is written for the stage after you find out.

## Article: Doom piles and doom boxes: the ADHD clutter cycle

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-doom-piles/
Published: 2026-10-22
Summary: The pile on the chair, the box of everything, the drawer you cannot open. Why ADHD produces doom piles, and how to clear one without a decluttering plan.

There is a chair. You know the one. It is not a chair any more, it is a geological record of the last four months, and the clean washing at the bottom of it has been through the machine twice without ever reaching a drawer.

ADHD communities call these doom piles, or doom boxes, and the usual expansion of the acronym is "didn't organise, only moved". That is exactly what they are: everything swept into one place to be dealt with later, except later has its own pile.

### Key takeaways

- A doom pile is what happens when putting things away requires more decisions than you have available.
- Making one is a reasonable short-term move; the problem is that it never gets reopened.
- The pile grows harder to approach the longer it sits, because it now represents failure as well as mess.
- Sorting by destination rather than by category is what gets a pile moving.
- Most of the long-term fix is reducing the number of homeless objects, not getting better at tidying.

### Why the pile forms

Putting a single object away is not one action. It is a decision about what the object is, a decision about where that kind of thing lives, a judgement about whether it is worth keeping, and then the physical act of carrying it there. For most objects that chain is trivial. For an ADHD brain, each link is a small executive cost, and a surface covered in forty objects is forty of those chains.

So you do the sensible thing under the circumstances and collapse forty decisions into one: everything goes in the box. The surface is clear. The room looks fine. You have bought yourself real relief, and nobody who has lived with this should feel bad about it, because the alternative on that day was not a tidy house, it was no progress at all.

The trouble is what the box becomes. It is now a container of forty undecided things with no deadline, which makes it exactly the sort of task that never gets started. And because the contents are random, you cannot do it in pieces without opening the whole thing.

Then the second layer arrives. The pile stops being just objects and becomes evidence: of the thing you did not deal with, the thing you keep not dealing with, and the person who keeps not dealing with it. Approaching it now costs more than it did at the start, because you have to get past the feeling first. That is why piles outlive the circumstances that created them.

> A doom pile is not a tidiness problem. It is forty deferred decisions in a container with no deadline.

### Clearing one

What works is removing the decisions, not steeling yourself to make them faster.

Sort by where things go, not by what they are. Four containers or four areas of floor is enough: things that leave the house, things that already have a home, things that have no home, and things that need an action. Every object goes into one of those without further thought. You are not deciding anything beyond destination, which turns forty judgement calls into forty sorting moves, and sorting is much cheaper than deciding.

Do the easy pile first. Everything with a home goes to its home immediately, which visibly shrinks the problem and gives you something that feels like progress within minutes.

Put a timer on it. Twenty minutes, then stop whether or not you are finished. A doom pile with no end time is just another open-ended task, and open-ended tasks are the reason it exists.

Do it with someone present if you can. Body doubling helps here more than almost anywhere else, partly because sorting is dull and partly because another person makes the emotional layer easier to get past.

And decide in advance what happens to the no-home pile, because that is where the process usually stalls. Either those objects get a home today, or they go in a labelled box with a date on it. A labelled box with a date is not another doom box, because it has a decision attached.

### Reducing the next one

Most of the long-term improvement comes from having fewer objects without a fixed address, rather than from tidying more often.

Give the recurring offenders a home that requires no thought: a hook by the door for keys, a dish for the things that come out of pockets, one drawer for cables. The objects that generate piles are usually the same twenty things over and over.

Keep a tray or bowl as a deliberate landing spot and empty it on a fixed day. A sanctioned pile with a scheduled end is a very different thing from an unsanctioned one that grows.

Lower the bar for what counts as putting something away. A clothes rail or a single basket for worn-but-not-dirty clothes solves the chair for a lot of people, because the chair exists precisely because those clothes have no category.

And accept that you will make more doom piles. The aim is shorter-lived ones, not none. A box you empty every fortnight is a working system. It only becomes a problem when it has no exit.

### Common questions

### What is a doom pile?

A doom pile, or doom box, is a pile or container of mixed items swept together to clear a surface quickly, intended to be sorted later. The acronym is usually given as "didn't organise, only moved". The term is widely used in ADHD communities.

### Why do people with ADHD make doom piles?

Because putting items away individually requires a chain of small decisions for every object, and executive function is the bottleneck. Collapsing many decisions into one action gives immediate relief. The difficulty is that the resulting pile is an open-ended task with no deadline, which is the kind that rarely gets started.

### How do I clear a doom pile?

Sort by destination rather than category: things that leave, things with a home, things without a home, and things needing an action. Put the easy ones away first, set a timer, and decide in advance what happens to the homeless items. Avoid trying to make keep-or-discard judgements on every object in one sitting.

### Is a doom box a bad thing?

Not inherently. As a short-term move it is a reasonable response to limited capacity, and it genuinely helps on a bad day. It becomes a problem when it has no scheduled end, because the contents stay undecided and the pile starts carrying guilt as well as objects.

### How do I stop making them?

Mostly by reducing the number of objects that have no fixed home, since the same items tend to generate piles repeatedly. A deliberate landing spot emptied on a fixed day also works well. [The ADHD Decision Reset](https://jmstruijk.com/books/adhd-decision-reset/) covers removing recurring decisions, which is the mechanism underneath this.

## Article: The ADHD tax: what it actually costs, and why budgeting advice keeps missing it

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-tax-what-it-costs/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: The ADHD tax is money lost to late fees, forgotten subscriptions and replacing things you own. Where it goes, and why budgeting advice misses it.

The phrase sounds like a joke until you sit down and add it up.

The ADHD tax is the money that leaves your account because of how your brain works, rather than because of anything you chose to buy. The late fee on a bill you had the money for. The second phone charger, because the first one is somewhere in the flat. The annual renewal for software you stopped using in March and cancelled in your head but never in the app. None of it was a decision. All of it was money.

I have paid this tax for most of my adult life, and for most of that time I thought it was a character problem. It took a late diagnosis and a lot of adding up to see it as a pattern with a shape, which is a far more useful thing to have.

### Key takeaways

- The ADHD tax is money lost to executive function, not to overspending on things you wanted.
- It hides in small amounts across many categories, which is exactly why it never shows up as a line in a budget.
- Shame keeps the number unknown, and an unknown number cannot be reduced.
- Systems that survive a bad week work. Systems that need you to remember do not.
- Counting it once, honestly, is usually the thing that changes the most.

### Where the money actually goes

When people picture ADHD and money, they picture impulse buys. Those are real, and I have written about them separately, but in my experience they are not where most of the money goes. The bigger drain is quieter.

Late fees and interest come first. Not because the money was missing, but because the bill arrived on a Tuesday when seventeen other things also arrived, and paying it required opening an app, finding a password, and holding a boring task in mind for ninety seconds. Multiply by every bill, every year.

Then there are subscriptions. Free trials that converted. Services you used properly for two months. The streaming thing somebody else set up on your card. Each one is small enough to feel not worth the friction of cancelling, and they compound precisely because each one is small enough to ignore.

Replacement costs are the category people underestimate most. Buying a thing you already own because you cannot find it, and finding it the week after. Food that goes off because it was bought with an optimistic plan attached. Clothes bought in a rush before an event because the ones you own are unwashed.

Then the avoidance costs. The letter you did not open. The tax deadline you missed by four days. The appointment you did not cancel in time. Avoidance has a price list, and it is usually worse than the thing you were avoiding.

And underneath all of it, the convenience premium. Paying more for the fast delivery, the pre-chopped version, the taxi, because the cheaper path had six steps in it and you had nothing left. Sometimes that premium is the correct purchase. It still counts.

### Why budgeting advice does not touch it

Most money advice assumes the problem is that you do not know where your money goes, or that you lack the discipline to stop spending it. So it offers information and restriction: track everything, set categories, cut back.

That advice works when the gap is between knowing and doing. The ADHD gap is somewhere else. It sits between intending and initiating. I have always known the bill was due. Knowing was never the missing piece.

Which is why "just set up a budget" lands the way it does. A budget is a document that requires daily maintenance from exactly the system that is already struggling. For a lot of us the spreadsheet is the thing we abandon in week two, and the abandonment then becomes more evidence for the story that we are the problem.

A system that depends on you remembering, at the right moment, to do a boring thing, is not a system. It is a test you will eventually fail, administered weekly, forever.

### The part nobody counts

Here is what I think makes the ADHD tax unusually expensive: the number is almost always unknown.

Most people I have spoken to about this have a rough feeling that it is "a few hundred a year" and a strong reluctance to check. The reluctance makes sense. Every entry on that list is a small piece of evidence that you failed at something ordinary, and nobody wants to sit with forty of those in a row.

So the total stays vague. And a vague number does two unhelpful things at once. It is small enough to dismiss, so nothing changes. And it is unbounded, so some part of you suspects it is catastrophic, which keeps the shame alive.

The one move that changed this for me was counting it. Once, properly, without editorialising. Three months of statements, every charge that was not a thing I meaningfully chose, written down with a date and an amount and no commentary.

It is an unpleasant afternoon. I would still call it the highest-return afternoon I have spent on my own finances, because afterwards the thing stops being a character flaw and becomes a number. Numbers have causes. Causes can be addressed one at a time.

> Shame makes the total vague, and a vague total cannot be reduced. The counting is the intervention.

### What actually reduces it

The pattern in everything that has worked for me is the same: remove the need to remember.

Automation does the heaviest lifting, and it is worth being systematic rather than enthusiastic about it. Every recurring bill on autopay, from an account that holds enough to cover it. This converts a recurring executive-function task into a one-time setup task, which is the trade our brains are built to win.

For subscriptions, the audit matters more than the vigilance. One pass through your card statement, cancelling everything you cannot immediately justify, beats a resolution to stay on top of it. You will not stay on top of it. I do this twice a year and I still find things.

Friction is worth placing deliberately. Card details removed from the devices where you shop worst. The one account that is hard to reach holding the money you are not supposed to touch. You are not trying to out-discipline yourself, you are trying to make the unwanted path slightly longer than your impulse lasts.

A single visible home for money matters more than the particular method. One place you can look to see what is true. It does not have to be elegant. Mine is not.

And for replacement costs, the fix is usually storage rather than willpower. One drawer for chargers. One hook for keys. The failure was never that you did not care about the charger, it is that the charger had no address.

### If you do one thing

Count the last three months.

Open your statements, write down anything that was a fee, a forgotten renewal, a replacement, or a late charge, and total it. Do not categorise it, do not judge it, do not plan yet. Just get the number.

Most people find it is larger than the feeling they had, and more fixable than they feared, because four or five sources usually account for the bulk of it. That is a tractable problem. The feeling of being bad with money is not.

If you would rather not do it on paper, the [ADHD Tax Calculator](https://jmstruijk.com/tools/adhd-tax-calculator/) walks through the same seven categories as the worksheet in the book and adds them up for you.

### Common questions

### Is the ADHD tax a real financial term?

No, and it is worth being clear about that. It is a community term, not a clinical or economic one. There is no official definition and nothing gets labelled this way on a statement. It is useful because it names a pattern that people with ADHD recognise instantly, which makes the pattern easier to talk about and easier to work on.

### Does this mean people with ADHD are bad with money?

It means executive function and money management overlap heavily, and ADHD affects executive function. Plenty of people with ADHD are thoughtful about money and still pay this tax, because the cost comes from initiation and follow-through rather than from values or intelligence. That distinction matters for choosing what to fix.

### How do I know if a purchase was impulsive or just convenient?

Ask whether you would make the same choice again knowing what it cost. Paying extra for a taxi at the end of a day when you had nothing left is often a reasonable trade. Paying extra for the same taxi every day because the alternative was never set up is a system problem wearing a convenience costume.

### Will medication fix the ADHD tax?

That is a question for a prescriber, not for me, and the answer varies a great deal between people. What I can say is that medication changes capacity, and systems change how much capacity a task requires. People I know who have found the most relief usually did both, and still needed the systems on the days capacity was low.

### Where should I start if the whole thing feels overwhelming?

Start with autopay on your three largest recurring bills, because late fees and interest tend to be the most expensive single category and the easiest to remove permanently. One afternoon of setup removes a recurring failure point for years. Everything else can wait until that is done.

## Article: Why ADHD brains overspend, and what actually helps

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/why-adhd-brains-overspend/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Impulsive spending with ADHD is rarely about wanting things. How reward, time and emotion drive it, and the fixes that actually work.

There is a particular feeling that comes about forty minutes after an online order goes through. The wanting has gone completely, and what has replaced it is a flat sort of confusion about who exactly made that decision.

If you recognise that, this article is for you. Impulsive spending with ADHD is usually explained as a lack of self-control, which is both unkind and unhelpful, because self-control is not the mechanism that failed.

### Key takeaways

- ADHD spending is usually driven by relief or stimulation rather than by wanting the object.
- A future cost feels much smaller than a present one, so comparing them honestly is harder.
- The gap between impulse and purchase has collapsed to about four seconds, and that gap is where restraint used to live.
- Rebuilding delay works better than trying to want things less.
- Most of the damage comes from a handful of repeating situations, which can be identified and interrupted.

### What is actually happening

Three things stack up, and they reinforce each other.

The first is that buying something produces a small, reliable hit of stimulation. For a brain that is chronically under-stimulated, that hit is doing a job. This is why the spending often clusters around boredom, and why the item itself can feel irrelevant within the hour. The purchase was never the point. The spike was.

The second is how differently a future cost registers. Everyone discounts the future to some degree, but with ADHD the discount is steep enough that forty pounds now and forty pounds in three weeks are not really the same number emotionally. The version of you who has to cover the shortfall is an abstraction. The relief is immediate and concrete. That comparison is not a fair fight.

The third is emotional regulation. A lot of ADHD spending happens on days that were already hard. After a difficult conversation, a humiliating meeting, a stretch of feeling behind on everything. Buying something is a fast, legal, socially acceptable way to change how you feel, and it works for about an hour. If you have ever noticed that your worst spending weeks map onto your worst weeks generally, that is not a coincidence.

Add rejection sensitivity and the pattern sharpens further. Spending on other people, picking up the bill, the generous gesture you cannot afford, is one of the most common forms this takes, and it is rarely discussed because it looks like kindness from the outside.

### Why the usual advice fails

Standard guidance is some version of wanting it less: be more disciplined, think about your goals, ask yourself whether you really need it.

That advice assumes the decision happens in a reflective state. The purchases I am describing do not. They happen in about four seconds, in a state where the reflective part of the system is not participating. Asking yourself whether you really need it requires you to be the kind of calm that the moment has already removed.

There is also a structural problem. Buying something now takes one thumb press. Historically there was friction everywhere: you had to go to a shop, during opening hours, with money. Every step was a chance for the impulse to pass. Saved cards, one-click ordering and same-day delivery have removed all of it.

The impulse has not got stronger. The distance it has to travel has got shorter.

> You cannot out-discipline a four-second gap. You can make it longer.

### What actually helps

Everything that has worked for me rebuilds some of that lost friction, or works on the state rather than the moment.

Start by taking your card details off the devices and sites where your spending is worst. Not all of them, because an unusable system gets abandoned. Just the two or three places where the damage actually happens. Having to find your wallet and type sixteen digits restores a few seconds of delay, and a surprising number of impulses do not survive it.

A waiting rule helps more than it sounds like it should, provided it is written down rather than held in your head. Anything above a threshold you set goes on a list with the date, and you are allowed to buy it after a fixed wait. You are not banning anything. You are only moving the decision to a moment when more of you is present. A good proportion of the list will look absurd by the time the wait is up, and the things that still look right are usually genuinely right.

It helps to keep spending money separate from money that has a job. One account that bills come out of, one account you are allowed to spend from. When the spending account is empty, that fact is visible without you having to do arithmetic you were never going to do.

Notifications on every transaction sound irritating and are. That is the point. The irritation reintroduces awareness at the moment of purchase rather than at the end of the month.

And when the spending is emotional, the substitution matters more than the restriction. If buying something is how you change your state after a bad day, removing it without replacing it leaves you with the bad day and no tools. Working out what else reliably shifts your state, and making that thing easier to reach than your phone, does more than any budget.

### Find your four situations

Most people's overspending is not spread evenly. It concentrates in a small number of repeating situations.

Look back over three months and find the purchases you regret. For each one, write down where you were, what time it was, and what had happened in the hours before. Patterns show up fast. Late evening, alone, tired. Immediately after a work humiliation. Sunday nights. Payday. In a shop with a particular person.

Four or five situations usually account for most of the money. That is a much smaller problem than being bad with money, and each situation can be interrupted on its own terms: a different route home, phone in another room after ten, a rule about shopping when hungry.

This is also why generic budgets fail for us. They treat spending as a uniform flow to be reduced, when it is a handful of specific moments to be designed around.

### A note on shame

Nearly everyone I have talked to about this carries a lot of shame about it, and the shame actively makes the spending worse.

The sequence runs the same way each time. You spend money you should not have. You feel awful. Feeling awful is a state you want to escape. The fastest escape available is the thing that caused it. It is a closed loop, and it runs on self-criticism rather than being corrected by it.

Breaking that loop is the single most useful thing I have done in this area, and it was not achieved by being kinder to myself in any vague sense. It came from treating each purchase as information about a situation rather than as evidence about my character. The situation can be changed. Character is harder to argue with, which is exactly why framing it that way keeps you stuck.

### Common questions

### Is impulsive spending an official ADHD symptom?

Impulsivity is one of the recognised features of ADHD, and spending is one of the places it shows up in adult life. You will not generally find overspending listed as a diagnostic criterion on its own. It is better understood as a common downstream consequence of impulsivity, emotional regulation difficulty and the way reward works in an ADHD brain.

### Does everyone with ADHD overspend?

No. Some people with ADHD underspend to the point of depriving themselves, often because they are so frightened of the pattern they see in themselves. Others have no particular difficulty with money at all. ADHD affects the machinery that money management runs on, which makes this more likely, not inevitable.

### Should I just cancel all my cards and use cash?

For some people cash works well, because physically handing over notes restores friction that cards remove. The risk is that an all-or-nothing system collapses the first time it becomes inconvenient, and then you have no system. Changing the two or three situations where most of your money actually goes tends to last longer than a total overhaul.

### How is this different from a shopping addiction?

There is overlap, and the line is not always obvious from the inside. The thing that usually distinguishes a compulsion is whether it continues despite serious consequences, whether it escalates, and whether stopping produces real distress. If any of that sounds familiar, it is worth raising with a professional rather than treating it as an ADHD systems problem.

### What should I set up first?

Separate your spending money from your committed money. Almost everything else works better once you can see, at a glance and without doing sums, how much is genuinely available to spend. If you want a structured version of that, it is the first thing [The ADHD Budget Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0G1HH2M25) sets up, and [The ADHD Budget Planner](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK4TZGF) is the undated version for keeping it running month to month.

## Article: ADHD and debt: why payoff plans keep failing, and what to do instead

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-debt-and-payoff-plans/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Debt payoff plans assume consistency, which ADHD does not reliably supply. Why the usual methods fail, and how to build one that survives a bad month.

Most debt advice is arithmetic, and the arithmetic is not wrong. List your debts, attack them in a sensible order, pay more than the minimum, repeat until finished.

The arithmetic has never been the part I failed at. I could explain the optimal method confidently while not opening a letter for six weeks.

If your debt has survived several serious attempts to clear it, the problem is probably not that you chose the wrong method.

### Key takeaways

- Standard payoff plans assume steady monthly action, which ADHD supplies unevenly.
- Avoidance is the most expensive single factor, and it grows the longer a thing goes unopened.
- Optimal plans are fragile, and a fragile plan that gets abandoned beats no plan only slightly.
- Automation beats intention, because it survives the weeks when you have nothing.
- One early visible win matters more than mathematical efficiency, because momentum is the scarce resource.

### Why the standard methods break

The two popular approaches are to pay the highest interest first, or to pay the smallest balance first for the psychological lift.

Both are fine on paper. Both assume you will look at your debts every month, decide an amount, make a payment, and keep doing that for two or three years without the system falling over.

That assumption is the whole problem. ADHD does not produce a flat line of effort. It produces bursts and troughs. In a burst you can do a year's worth of financial admin in one evening. In a trough you cannot open an envelope. A plan that needs a constant monthly input is designed for a kind of consistency that is not available, and the first missed month usually ends it, because a missed month is evidence of failure and evidence of failure produces avoidance.

The plans are not badly designed. They are designed for a different machine.

### Avoidance is the expensive part

If I had to name the single thing that has cost me most money, it is not interest rates. It is unopened post.

The mechanism is familiar to anyone who has lived it. A letter arrives that is probably bad. Opening it would produce a feeling you do not have the capacity for today, so it goes on a pile. The next day it is slightly worse, because now it is both the original problem and evidence that you avoided it. The pile gets harder to approach in proportion to how long it has been there, and the thing inside is quietly accruing fees the whole time.

The cruel detail is that the contents are almost always less bad than the pile suggests. Most creditors would rather arrange something than escalate. The fees that accumulate during avoidance frequently exceed what the original problem would have cost to resolve.

Knowing this does not dissolve the avoidance, because avoidance is not an information deficit. What helps is reducing what opening the thing requires: doing it with another person in the room, doing all of it in one sitting rather than one letter at a time, or having a fixed slot where the task has a beginning and an end.

> The pile is almost always worse than its contents. The cost is in the waiting, not in the letter.

### Build a plan that survives a bad month

The design goal is different from the usual one. You are not optimising for the fastest payoff under ideal conditions. You are optimising for a plan that is still running in eight months, including the months where you are not functioning well.

Automate the minimums first, before anything else. Every debt, automatic payment, minimum amount, from an account that will cover it. This is the floor. It means a bad month costs you progress but does not cost you fees, a default, or a mark on your credit file. The floor matters more than the ceiling, because the floor is what holds when you are not there.

Then make extra payments manual and opportunistic. Counterintuitive, but the bursts are real and worth using. When a good week arrives, throw money at the target debt. Do not commit in advance to an aggressive monthly figure that assumes every month is a good one. Committing to the maximum means failing most months, and failing most months ends plans.

Pick one target debt at a time, and pick the one that will clear soonest. Mathematically this is usually not optimal. It is still what I would recommend, because closing an account produces a visible, final result, and visible results are the fuel that keeps the thing going. An approach that is five percent more efficient and gets abandoned in month four loses to a slightly worse approach that survives.

Keep a single sheet showing every debt, the balance, and the minimum, and put it somewhere you will physically see it. Not a spreadsheet you have to open. A piece of paper. Out of sight genuinely does mean out of mind here, and most of the avoidance happens in the gap between knowing a thing exists and being able to look at it.

Finally, give yourself a defined review slot, once a month, with a time limit. Twenty minutes, diarised. The limit matters as much as the slot, because an open-ended financial review is exactly the kind of task that gets postponed forever.

### Talk to the people you owe

This is the piece most people skip, and it tends to produce the largest single improvement.

Creditors have hardship processes. Interest can sometimes be frozen, payments reduced, plans arranged. None of that is advertised prominently, and all of it generally requires you to ask.

Making that call is unpleasant. It involves admitting to a stranger that you are struggling, usually several times, usually on hold. I have found it helps to write down what to say first, because the conversation tends to produce the kind of shame that makes it hard to think, and reading a prepared sentence is easier than composing one.

If the debt is substantial, a free debt advice service is worth more than anything I can write here. They negotiate for a living, they know what each creditor will actually agree to, and they do not charge. Avoid anyone who wants a fee to manage your debt.

### The shame loop again

Debt and shame are wound together tightly enough that it is hard to work on one without the other.

The loop is predictable. Avoiding the debt makes it worse. The debt getting worse produces more shame. More shame produces more avoidance. The person inside that loop looks, from outside, like someone who does not care, when in fact the loop runs on caring too much to look.

The way out that worked for me was a plain one. Debt is a number, arrived at through a combination of circumstances, choices and an undiagnosed condition that made a particular set of mistakes very likely. It is not a verdict. Treating it as a verdict is what keeps the envelope closed, and the envelope staying closed is what makes it grow.

### Common questions

### Should I use the snowball or avalanche method with ADHD?

Smallest balance first, in most cases. The avalanche method saves more in interest, but it can be a long time before anything visibly completes, and sustained invisible progress is hard for an ADHD brain to stay attached to. Clearing an account entirely gives you a result you can see, and that tends to keep the plan alive.

### What if I cannot even look at my debts?

Start with the total rather than the details. One session, one page, every balance written down with nothing else required of you. No plan, no calls, no decisions. Knowing the real number is usually less frightening than the imagined one, and the imagined one is what avoidance feeds on.

### Does ADHD make debt more likely?

It affects the systems that keep debt from accumulating: paying on time, tracking balances, resisting impulse purchases, opening post, planning ahead. None of that is destiny, and plenty of people with ADHD carry no debt at all. It does mean that when debt appears, it often has more to do with executive function than with income.

### Will a debt management plan hurt my credit?

It can, and the specifics depend on the type of arrangement and where you live. A free debt advice service will explain the trade-offs for your situation, which is exactly the sort of question worth asking someone qualified rather than reading about. Missed payments and defaults also affect credit, so doing nothing is rarely the neutral option it feels like.

### Where should I start today?

Set up automatic minimum payments on everything. One afternoon, and it removes the most expensive failure mode permanently. [The ADHD Debt Payoff Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HDK1RYSW) walks through the rest of this process step by step if you want the structured version.

## Article: Hyperfocus without the crash: using the good days without paying for them twice

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-hyperfocus-without-burnout/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Hyperfocus gets called an ADHD superpower, usually right before it costs you a week. How it works, and how to use it without the crash.

Someone will eventually tell you that hyperfocus is your superpower. They usually mean well, and they have usually only seen the first half.

The first half is remarkable. Eleven hours disappear. The work is better than anything you produce on an ordinary day, and it arrives faster. You forget to eat and do not care.

The second half is the part that does not make it into the motivational post. Two or three days where your brain is a wet towel, you cannot answer a simple email, and the thing you built so brilliantly on Tuesday sits untouched because approaching it now feels physically impossible.

### Key takeaways

- Hyperfocus is not controllable attention. It is attention that has locked on and will not release.
- The productive stretch and the crash that follows are one event, so the output is never free.
- The cost comes mostly from skipped maintenance, not from the hours themselves.
- Hyperfocus cannot reliably be summoned, which makes it a terrible thing to build a schedule on.
- Interrupting it on purpose, before exhaustion, is what makes it usable repeatedly.

### What hyperfocus actually is

It is easy to mistake hyperfocus for concentration doing what you want. It behaves more like the opposite.

Ordinary attention can be directed and released. You decide to work on something, you work on it, you stop for lunch, you come back. Hyperfocus removes the release. Something catches, and then disengaging becomes extremely difficult, including when you want to disengage, including when continuing is obviously a bad idea.

That is why it so rarely lands on the thing you most need to do. You cannot point it. It attaches to whatever is novel, interesting or urgent enough, which might be the project due Friday, or might be researching a holiday you are not taking. The quality of the attention is identical. The usefulness varies enormously.

It also quietly turns off the signals that normally pace you. Hunger, thirst, needing the toilet, the ache that tells you to stand up, the sense that it is getting late. Those are not overridden by willpower. They mostly fail to arrive.

### Why the crash happens

The crash gets blamed on the hours, and the hours are part of it. Mostly, though, it comes from what did not happen during them.

Across eleven hours of hyperfocus, a typical session skips most meals, most water, every break, and whatever sleep would have happened at the end. It also runs a sustained level of cognitive effort with no recovery intervals. Any brain would be depleted afterwards. The ADHD version adds a dopamine spike that ends abruptly, and the flatness afterwards is steeper for the height.

There is a second cost that compounds. While you were inside the session, ordinary life continued. Post arrived. Messages went unanswered. The kitchen got worse. So the crash is not only depletion, it is depletion plus a visible backlog that accumulated while you were gone, arriving exactly when you have the least capacity to face it.

This is how a brilliant Tuesday produces a worse week than no Tuesday at all.

> The output is real. It is just never free, and the invoice arrives later.

### Using it without the full price

I have stopped trying to control when hyperfocus arrives. Nothing I have tried produces it on demand, and treating it as summonable leads to planning around something that may not show up.

What does work is changing what happens during and after.

The most useful single habit is a hard external interrupt. A timer in another room, set for ninety minutes, loud enough that stopping it means standing up. The point is not to end the session. It is to create a moment where you are vertical and your body can report in. Often you will drink something and sit back down, and that is fine. Occasionally you will realise it is nine at night and you have not eaten, which is the information you could not otherwise access.

Set the conditions before you start, not during. Water on the desk, something edible within reach, phone somewhere you can hear it. Once hyperfocus engages, you will not get up to fetch any of this, so it has to be in place beforehand.

Stop before the fuel runs out, not when it does. This is the hardest habit on the list and the one that changes most. Ending a session with something left makes the next day survivable and makes returning to the work possible. Riding it to complete depletion is what buys the three-day crash, and it also makes the work itself harder to re-approach, because your brain now associates it with feeling terrible.

Plan the day after as a low-capacity day rather than hoping it will not be one. If Tuesday was a fourteen-hour session, Wednesday is for small, undemanding, already-defined tasks. Scheduling anything important the day after a big session is a reliable way to fail at it and then feel bad about that too.

And when you come out of a session, leave yourself a note about where you were and what comes next. Future you has no memory of your mental state and no capacity to reconstruct it. One paragraph saves an hour.

### If you are building something on the side

The reason this matters commercially is that side projects run on exactly this pattern, and the pattern can either compound or eat itself.

The failure mode is familiar. A burst of enormous progress, a crash, a fortnight of nothing, guilt about the fortnight, another burst driven partly by that guilt. From outside it looks like inconsistency. From inside it feels like being unable to rely on yourself.

Two things make this survivable. The first is designing the work so a burst produces something complete rather than something half-built, because half-built things decay during the troughs and are hard to re-enter. The second is making the minimum viable version of the work small enough to do on a bad day, so the troughs produce slow progress instead of zero progress and the associated guilt.

Consistency is not the ADHD strength. Intensity is. A project that converts intensity into finished units, and that survives the gaps between them, plays to what you actually have.

### Common questions

### Is hyperfocus unique to ADHD?

No. Deep absorption in an engaging task is something most people experience, and it is also commonly described by autistic people. What tends to be distinctive in ADHD is the difficulty disengaging, the way it lands on things you did not choose, and the loss of bodily signals during it. The experience sits on a spectrum rather than belonging to one group.

### Can I train myself to hyperfocus on demand?

I have not found a reliable way, and I am sceptical of anyone selling one. You can make the conditions more likely by removing interruptions and working on something genuinely interesting with a near deadline. What you cannot do is guarantee it, which is why building a schedule that depends on it tends to end badly.

### Is hyperfocus a good thing or a bad thing?

It is a capability with a cost attached, and the ratio depends almost entirely on what it lands on and whether you manage the aftermath. Pointed at work that matters, with breaks and a recovery day planned, it produces things that would otherwise not exist. Pointed at something irrelevant for fourteen hours, it takes a week and gives nothing back.

### Why can I hyperfocus on hobbies but not on work?

Because interest and urgency are what engage it, and most work is neither. This is one of the more painful parts of ADHD, and it is frequently misread by other people as choosing to care about the wrong things. Making a work task more concrete, more novel, or more immediately deadlined sometimes helps. Sometimes nothing does, and the task has to be done the slow, effortful way.

### How do I recover faster from a crash?

Treat it as recovery rather than as a failure to be pushed through. Food, water, sleep, and low-demand tasks. Fighting a crash with more effort generally extends it. If the crashes are becoming longer, more frequent, or are not lifting at all, that is worth taking seriously as possible burnout rather than as ordinary tiredness.

## Article: Diagnosed with ADHD as an adult: what the first year is actually like

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/adhd-diagnosis-as-an-adult-first-year/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: Relief, grief, and rereading your own life. What the first year after a late ADHD diagnosis tends to be like, and what helps.

Nobody warns you about the grief.

They warn you about the waiting lists and the paperwork and the possibility of being told no. Nobody mentions that a few weeks after you are told yes, you will be sitting somewhere ordinary, reconstructing a school report from twenty years ago, and find yourself genuinely upset about a child who was told to apply himself.

A late diagnosis is good news. It is also a specific kind of loss, and the two arrive together.

### Key takeaways

- Relief usually comes first, then grief, and the grief catches most people off guard.
- Rereading your own history is the main work of the first year.
- Telling people goes less well than you expect, and that is about them, not about you.
- Medication is a tool with a trial period, not a verdict on whether you are really ADHD.
- Most of the practical gains come later, once the emotional part has somewhere to sit.

### The first few weeks

The relief is enormous and slightly manic. There is a reason. There has been a reason the whole time.

Most people go through a phase of reading everything. Forums, books, videos, other people's accounts, usually at two in the morning. Every description lands. You keep finding sentences that seem to have been written about you specifically, and the recognition is a genuinely good feeling after years of not having a frame that fit.

There is often a burst of energy with it. Plans get made. Systems get bought. You are going to fix everything now that you know.

This phase is useful, and it is worth knowing that the plans made during it are usually too ambitious. Mine were. The energy is real, but it is partly the relief talking, and the relief does not stay at that level.

### Then the grief

It tends to arrive a few weeks or months in, often without warning, and the common reaction is to feel foolish about it. You got an answer. Why are you upset?

Because an answer is also a reframe of everything that came before it. The jobs you left. The friendships that went quiet because you did not reply for four months. The repeated, patient feedback that you had potential and were not applying it. The things people said about you that you accepted, because enough people said them that they looked like facts.

Rereading all of that with new information is the actual work of the first year, and it is heavier than anyone tells you. There is anger in it, often directed at people who should have noticed, which is complicated because they usually could not have. There is a specific sadness about the version of you who tried very hard at something that was never going to work the way it was being attempted.

Grief is the right word for it. It behaves like grief, it takes roughly as long, and it does not respond well to being hurried.

> You are not grieving a diagnosis. You are grieving the time spent explaining yourself with the wrong information.

### Telling people

This goes less smoothly than most people expect, and it is worth being prepared.

The responses that sting are rarely hostile. They are casual. Everyone is a bit ADHD these days. You seem fine to me. Isn't that just an excuse. You went to university, so it cannot be that bad. Most of these come from people who mean no harm and have no idea what they are dismissing.

A few things made this easier for me. Deciding in advance who actually needs to know, rather than announcing it generally while the relief is still high. Having one or two plain sentences ready, so you are not composing an explanation in the moment. And accepting that some people will simply not take it on board, and that their not understanding does not alter what is true.

Finding other late-diagnosed adults matters more than almost any other single thing here. Not for advice. For the specific relief of describing something strange and particular and having someone say yes, that, without needing it explained.

### Medication, if you go that way

This is a conversation for a prescriber, and the right choice differs enormously between people, so I will keep to what I can say honestly.

It is a trial, not a test. If the first thing does not work, or the dose is wrong, or the side effects are not acceptable, that is information rather than a verdict on whether your diagnosis was real. Plenty of people go through more than one option before finding something useful, and plenty decide against it entirely and do fine.

It also does not do what people imagine. The common description is a quieter head rather than a transformed life. Skills you never built do not appear because of a tablet. Systems still have to be built. What changes for many people is how much capacity there is available to build them.

### What helps in the first year

Go slower than the relief wants you to. The urge to overhaul everything in month one is strong and usually produces a pile of abandoned systems that then function as fresh evidence of failure.

Keep notes about yourself. Specific things you notice about how you work, when you crash, what sets off what. This is the raw material for every system you will build later, and you cannot reconstruct it afterwards from memory.

Choose one area and work on it for a season. Sleep, or money, or the thing that is currently doing the most damage. Not all of them at once.

Expect a flat period. A lot of people hit a dip around six to nine months in, when the explanation has stopped being new and the work of actually living differently has started. That dip is normal and does not mean the diagnosis was wrong or that you have wasted the opportunity.

And let the grief have room rather than trying to be grateful on schedule. It moves faster when it is allowed to happen than when it is argued with.

### Common questions

### Is it worth getting diagnosed as an adult?

For most people I have spoken to, yes, though for varied reasons. Some want access to medication. Some want workplace or study accommodations. Many want the explanation itself, which turns out to be worth more than expected. The main arguments against are cost, waiting times, and the fact that a diagnosis does not by itself change anything practical.

### Why was it missed when I was a child?

Commonly because childhood ADHD was understood more narrowly than it is now, and because the quiet, inattentive presentation does not disrupt a classroom. Children who were academically capable, or who masked well, or who were girls, were particularly likely to be overlooked. Being missed says something about the screening of the time rather than about the severity of your experience.

### Is late-diagnosis grief normal?

It is extremely common, and it is one of the least discussed parts of the process. Relief and grief coexisting is the usual pattern rather than a contradiction. If the low mood is persistent, deepening, or affecting your ability to function, that is worth raising with a professional, because late diagnosis also tends to surface things that were being managed by not looking too closely.

### How long does the adjustment take?

Most accounts I have encountered describe something like a year to feel settled, with the emotional work front-loaded and the practical gains arriving later. There is no schedule, and people who take longer have not done it wrong.

### What should I actually do first?

Nothing structural for a few weeks. Read, notice, write things down, and find other late-diagnosed adults. The systems work lands much better once the emotional ground has settled, which is why [The Late-Diagnosed ADHD Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBLVP38R) starts with the rereading rather than with the productivity.

## Article: Finding out you are autistic in adulthood

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/autistic-in-adulthood-late-diagnosis/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: What changes when you find out in your thirties or forties that you are autistic, why so many adults are missed, and what the first months involve.

It rarely starts with a doctor. For most people I have spoken to, it starts with a video, or a thread, or a friend's offhand comment, and then a long quiet period of reading at night without telling anyone.

The first reaction is usually to dismiss it. You do not look autistic, by which you mean you do not resemble the narrow version you were shown growing up. You have friends. You can hold a conversation. You made eye contact with someone this week.

Then you read a description of sensory overload, or of what a social event costs afterwards, and something you assumed was universal turns out to be specific.

### Key takeaways

- Most late-identified autistic adults have been masking so long that the mask reads as personality.
- The old diagnostic picture missed anyone who was verbal, academically able, or socially motivated.
- Self-identification is widely accepted in autistic communities, and formal assessment is expensive and slow in many places.
- The first months are mostly reinterpretation, not change.
- Sensory needs are usually the fastest practical improvement available.

### Why you were missed

The description that most adults alive today were measured against was built from observations of young boys with obvious, visible differences. If you were verbal, did well at school, and wanted friends, you did not resemble that description and nobody looked further.

Masking is the other half of it. If you worked out early that copying other people produced better outcomes than being yourself, you got good at it, and the better you got the less anyone saw. Many late-identified adults were praised throughout childhood for exactly the behaviour that was concealing them. Being described as mature for your age, or sensitive, or a bit of an old soul, often turns out to mean something else in retrospect.

Women, non-binary people, and anyone who was socially motivated enough to study people deliberately were missed at much higher rates. So were people whose difficulties got filed under anxiety, depression, or an eating disorder, which were treated for years with limited effect because the underlying thing was never addressed.

### The reinterpretation

The work of the first months is not change. It is going back through your own history with a different lens.

The exhaustion after social events that you assumed was introversion and could never quite square with the fact that you liked the people. The specific clothing you have always bought, which you thought of as a preference and now looks like a sensory requirement. The jobs that went wrong for reasons you could never explain properly. The childhood interests that were so consuming other people found them strange, and which you learned to talk about less.

Food comes up for almost everyone. Textures, temperatures, the same meal for years, a short list of things that are safe. Most people had this filed under fussiness, usually because that is what they were told.

So does the lifelong sense of running a translation layer. Watching how others do things, copying it, checking the result, adjusting. Many late-identified adults describe realising that other people are not doing this, which is a genuinely disorienting thing to learn in your forties.

> The mask is not something you put on. By the time you find out, it is most of what you think you are.

### The part that is hard

The relief is real and it is not the whole story.

There is anger, often at the places that were supposed to notice. There is grief for the decades spent trying to fix things that were never faults. There is a specific loneliness in realising that the effort you have been making invisibly was both enormous and unacknowledged, because the entire point of masking was that nobody could tell.

Identity gets unstable for a while. If a large portion of your behaviour was learned camouflage, working out what is underneath takes time, and the question of who you would have been without it has no answer. It is worth sitting with anyway.

And there is an awkward practical problem. Once you know, the mask becomes harder to hold. Many people find their tolerance for environments they used to survive drops sharply after identification. That is usually interpreted as getting worse. It is more often the end of a very long unconscious effort, which is not the same thing.

### Assessment, if you want one

Whether to pursue a formal diagnosis is genuinely a personal decision, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you need it for.

Formal assessment can matter for workplace adjustments, educational support, and in some places access to services. It can also provide a certainty that self-identification does not, which matters to some people a great deal.

The costs are real. Long waits in public systems, significant expense privately, and clinicians who vary in how well they recognise adults who mask. Some people go through assessment and are told no by someone working from an outdated picture, which is painful and does not settle the question.

Self-identification is accepted in most autistic communities and is a legitimate position, particularly given that access to assessment is unevenly distributed. You do not need anyone's permission to understand yourself accurately.

### What helps early

Sensory changes give the fastest return. Loop earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones, lower lighting, clothing chosen for how it feels rather than how it looks, a room at home that is quiet and dim and nobody else's. These are small, cheap, and often make a noticeable difference within days, which matters when everything else is in flux.

Recovery time needs to be scheduled rather than hoped for. If a social event costs you a day, that day is part of the event, and planning as though it is not is how people end up in a deficit they cannot explain.

Stimming, if you suppressed it, is worth letting back in. Most late-identified adults were trained out of visible self-regulation young, and getting it back tends to help more than expected.

Reading autistic adults rather than clinical material is the other thing I would recommend without hesitation. The clinical literature describes autism from outside, in terms of deficits observable to other people. Autistic writers describe it from inside, and that is the version that is actually useful for living.

### Common questions

### Can you become autistic as an adult?

No. Autism is lifelong and present from early development. What happens in adulthood is recognition rather than onset. People frequently find, once they look, that the evidence was there throughout childhood and was interpreted as something else at the time.

### Is self-diagnosis valid?

It is widely accepted within autistic communities, particularly given the cost and waiting times for formal assessment and the number of adults turned away by clinicians working from an outdated picture. Formal diagnosis still matters for accommodations and services in many places. Both things can be true at once.

### What is the difference between being autistic and being introverted?

Introversion is about where your energy comes from and is one trait among many. Autism involves differences in sensory processing, communication, social intuition, and a need for predictability, and it is present across every part of life rather than only in social settings. Plenty of autistic people are sociable and still find socialising expensive in a way introversion does not explain.

### Why do I feel worse since finding out?

This is extremely common and usually reflects the end of unconscious masking rather than a decline. Once you know what you have been doing, holding it becomes harder, and the full cost of it becomes visible for the first time. Many people describe a period of reduced tolerance before things stabilise.

### Where do I start?

Sensory changes, because they are immediate and cheap, and reading autistic authors rather than clinical descriptions. [The Late-Diagnosed Autistic Workbook](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBNKNWZC) is built around that order, starting with sensory needs and masking before anything else.

## Article: AuDHD: what it is like being autistic and ADHD at the same time

URL: https://jmstruijk.com/blog/audhd-autistic-and-adhd/
Published: 2026-10-21
Summary: AuDHD means being both autistic and ADHD. The two sets of needs pull against each other, which is why advice for either one alone tends to fail.

For a long time these two were not allowed to coexist. Diagnostic rules in several countries actively prevented clinicians from recording both, which means a generation of people were given whichever label was noticed first and sent away with half an explanation.

That changed. Plenty of us had already spent decades finding that advice for one condition kept failing in ways that advice for the other would have predicted.

AuDHD is the informal term for being both. It is not two conditions sitting side by side, politely taking turns. The interaction produces something with its own shape.

### Key takeaways

- AuDHD is autism and ADHD together, and the two sets of needs frequently contradict each other.
- Advice written for either condition alone tends to fail, because following it worsens the other side.
- The contradictions can make people appear less affected than they are, which delays identification.
- Burnout tends to arrive harder, because both sets of demands are being managed at once.
- Designing for the conflict directly works better than picking a side.

### The contradiction

The central experience is wanting two incompatible things with equal sincerity.

One part of you needs routine, predictability, and sameness. The same meal, the same route, the same sequence, because deviation is genuinely costly. The other part is bored to the point of pain by exactly that sameness and will sabotage it for novelty.

So you build a beautiful system. It works. The autistic part relaxes into the structure, which is a real relief. Then around week three the ADHD part has had enough, the system becomes intolerable, and you abandon something that was working perfectly well for reasons you cannot defend.

This happens with food, with work, with sleep, with hobbies, with the layout of a room. It is the defining pattern.

Social life runs on the same fault line. You want contact and you want to be left alone, often within the same hour. Socialising is draining in the autistic way and sought out in the ADHD way, which produces a cycle of overcommitting, enjoying it, and then needing to vanish for a fortnight.

Planning is similar. A real need to know what is happening next, and a complete inability to reliably do the thing that was planned.

> The usual advice fails because it was written for one half. Follow it faithfully and you make the other half worse.

### Why it goes unnoticed

The two sides partially cancel out, which makes AuDHD people look more functional than they are.

The ADHD chaos is dampened by autistic systems and rule-following, so you are not as visibly disorganised as ADHD alone would predict. The autistic rigidity is softened by ADHD flexibility and distractibility, so you are not as visibly rigid as autism alone would predict. From outside, neither picture is complete, so neither gets investigated.

What shows up instead is cost. Anxiety, depression, exhaustion, a sense of working extraordinarily hard for ordinary results. Those get treated, sometimes for years, with mixed results, because the treatment is aimed at the smoke.

The other reason is sequencing. Many people get one diagnosis, work hard on it, and find that a stubborn remainder does not respond. That remainder is frequently the other condition. If you have been told you have ADHD and the ADHD strategies only partly work, or you have been identified as autistic and your life is still chaotic in ways autism does not explain, it is worth considering.

### What actually helps

The approach that works is designing for the conflict rather than pretending one side will eventually win.

Build structures with variety inside them. Fixed frame, flexible contents. A set meal time with a rotating set of options. A fixed working block where what you work on varies. This satisfies the need for predictability without triggering the boredom response, and it is the single most useful principle I have found.

Keep several systems in rotation rather than searching for the perfect one. Expect to abandon the current method every few weeks, and plan for the abandonment instead of treating it as failure. Two or three systems you cycle between will outlast one system you believe in.

Protect the non-negotiable sensory things absolutely, and let the novelty happen elsewhere. Sensory overload does not become more tolerable because the ADHD side wants excitement. Keep the environment stable and let the stimulation come from ideas, projects or people.

Make rest more specific than the word suggests. Autistic recovery usually means low sensory input and no demands. ADHD recovery usually means stimulation and novelty. Doing one when you need the other leaves you unrested, and most people have to learn to tell the difference deliberately, because both register vaguely as tiredness.

Shrink transitions wherever you can. Switching tasks is costly for the autistic side and the ADHD side both, for different reasons, which makes it unusually expensive for AuDHD people. Fewer, longer blocks beat a day full of context switches.

### About burnout

It is worth saying plainly that AuDHD burnout tends to be severe.

You are running both sets of demands at once. The masking, the sensory management, the social translation, plus the constant executive effort of initiating, remembering, and finishing.
